World.title: Costa Rica Reports Renewed Increase in COVID-19 Cases
World.content:
COVID-19 has once again become the most widely circulating respiratory virus detected in Costa Rica, as health officials urge residents to take basic precautions amid an increase in cases and hospitalizations. The latest epidemiological surveillance places COVID-19 ahead of rhinovirus and parainfluenza among respiratory viruses currently circulating here.

During epidemiological week 29, covering July 13 through July 19, Costa Rica recorded 126 confirmed COVID-19 cases, up from 94 the previous week. That represents an increase of about 34%. Hospitalizations also climbed, with 29 COVID-19 patients receiving hospital care compared with 18 the previous week, an increase of roughly 56%. Five deaths associated with COVID-19 were reported during the same epidemiological week.

The figures remain far below the levels Costa Rica experienced during the height of the pandemic, and there is currently no national health alert for respiratory illnesses. However, the change in circulation has prompted renewed attention as several respiratory viruses spread simultaneously.

Costa Rica has recorded more than 771,000 cases of respiratory illness so far this year, a broader figure that includes illnesses caused by multiple viruses rather than COVID-19 alone. Children, older adults and people with chronic health conditions remain among those considered most vulnerable to complications from respiratory infections.

Health authorities are recommending many of the familiar measures used to reduce respiratory infections: keeping vaccinations current, washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes and choosing well-ventilated spaces when possible. People experiencing respiratory symptoms are also being encouraged to avoid crowded activities and limit close contact with vulnerable relatives or friends until they recover.

The renewed circulation of COVID-19 comes during Costa Rica’s rainy season, when respiratory illnesses can become more noticeable as people spend more time indoors and several viruses circulate at the same time. For residents and travelers, the latest numbers do not signal a return to pandemic-era restrictions. There have been no announcements of renewed mask mandates, travel requirements or widespread restrictions connected to the current increase.

Instead, the emphasis remains on individual precautions, particularly for people at greater risk of serious illness. Health officials continue to monitor COVID-19 alongside influenza, rhinovirus, parainfluenza and other respiratory illnesses to identify changes in circulation and hospital demand.

World.title: Gunmen Storm Costa Rica Hospital and Kill Patient in Nicoya
World.content:
Two masked gunmen forced their way into a public hospital in Guanacaste early Saturday and shot a patient to death as he lay on a stretcher in the observation area, in an unusually brazen attack that has prompted tighter security at the facility. The shooting occurred between approximately 3:05 a.m. and 3:10 a.m. at Hospital La Anexión in Nicoya.

The attackers arrived by car carrying long guns believed to be AR-15-style rifles. They threatened a hospital security guard, entered the building and went directly to the area where the patient was being treated. The victim, identified by the surnames Valverde Matarrita, was 32 years old. He was shot multiple times in the face and chest and died at the hospital.

Valverde Matarrita had been admitted approximately two days earlier for an injury to one of his legs and remained under observation when the gunmen entered the facility. An elderly woman was also struck by gunfire during the attack. She suffered a gunshot wound to the buttock but was reported in stable condition, and the injury was not considered life-threatening.

Authorities have since revealed that Valverde Matarrita previously had police protection ordered by prosecutors in Guanacaste. That protection, however, had been withdrawn before Saturday’s attack. Officials have not yet explained publicly why the protection was removed or why the victim may have been targeted.

Police started an operation to locate the attackers following the shooting. The car used in the escape has been found by authorities, but no arrests had been announced as of Saturday afternoon. The Judicial Investigation Agency, known as the OIJ, is investigating the killing. The Costa Rican Social Security Fund, which operates the public hospitals, reinforced security at Hospital La Anexión following the attack. Hospital services continued operating normally Saturday.

The shooting is particularly brazen because the attackers were willing to enter an operating medical facility, threaten security personnel and move through the hospital to reach their intended target. Hospital La Anexión is one of the main public medical centers serving Nicoya and surrounding communities on the Nicoya Peninsula, including an area heavily visited by foreign tourists and home to a sizable expatriate population.

The attack adds another security concern for Guanacaste, where authorities have been confronting violent crime linked to disputes between criminal groups in parts of the province. For the hospital, the immediate issue is how two heavily armed men were able to get inside the facility and reach a patient. Security has already been strengthened while investigators work to reconstruct the attack and identify those responsible.

No motive for the killing had been announced by Saturday afternoon.

World.title: Why the Cincinnati Open Is the Last Major Test Before the US Open
World.content:
The Cincinnati Open begins opening its grounds to fans this weekend, but for the players arriving in Mason, Ohio, the tournament carries considerably more weight than another stop on the summer schedule. Cincinnati is the final ATP Masters 1000 and WTA 1000 tournament before the US Open, making the next two weeks one of the clearest tests of who is ready to contend in New York and who still has work to do.



Qualifying begins August 11 at the Lindner Family Tennis Center, followed by the men’s and women’s main draws on August 13. The Cincinnati singles finals will be played August 23. Exactly one week later, on August 30, the US Open singles main draws begin in New York. That short turnaround is what gives Cincinnati its importance.

Players who make deep runs will arrive at Flushing Meadows with confidence, match fitness and proof that their games are working on North American hard courts. Those struggling with injuries, form or the transition from other surfaces have little time left to make adjustments.

Cincinnati Offers a Grand Slam-Level Test

Cincinnati is not a Grand Slam, but the quality of competition makes it one of the closest things players will encounter before New York. The men’s tournament is an ATP Masters 1000 event and the women’s competition carries WTA 1000 status. Both feature 96-player singles draws filled with many of the highest-ranked players in the world.

A Masters 1000 title on the men’s side is worth 1,000 ranking points, while the tournament also offers substantial ranking opportunities throughout the draw. But Cincinnati’s value goes beyond points.

Players will face many of the same opponents they could encounter a week later at the US Open, often under demanding summer conditions. Long matches, heat, humidity and repeated days of competition provide a useful indication of who is physically prepared for a two-week Grand Slam.

It also gives players another chance to solve problems that became apparent earlier in the North American hard-court season. A serve that was effective on another surface may not produce the same results. A player struggling to defend a second serve or finish short balls has very little time remaining to correct those weaknesses.

By Cincinnati, experimentation begins to give way to urgency.

Hard Courts Change the Equation

The transition to North American hard courts is particularly important because the US Open rewards a different combination of skills than the European clay and grass seasons that dominate the preceding months. Movement changes. Points can develop more quickly. First serves and returns become increasingly important, and players who can take control of the baseline early are often rewarded.

For players who built much of their season on clay, Cincinnati can provide an especially revealing test. That makes the tournament worth watching closely for Latin American tennis fans. Brazil’s João Fonseca, Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo, Sebastián Báez and Tomás Martín Etcheverry, Peru’s Ignacio Buse and Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo are among the players from the region heading into the Cincinnati period with the US Open approaching.

Colombia’s Camila Osorio leads the Latin American presence on the women’s side, with other players from the region attempting to reach the main draw through qualifying. The question for each is not simply how far they can advance in Ohio. Cincinnati will provide another measure of how well their games are translating to the surface they will encounter in New York.

Ranking Points Matter, But So Does the Draw

Cincinnati can also change a player’s position heading into the final Grand Slam of the season. A deep run at a 1000-level tournament can produce a substantial rankings boost, particularly for players clustered closely together in the standings. That matters because rankings help determine seedings and ultimately influence the path a player may face through a major tournament.

For someone near one of those dividing lines, a strong Cincinnati performance can have consequences beyond the tournament itself. The difference between being seeded and unseeded at a Grand Slam can mean avoiding one of the world’s highest-ranked players in the opening rounds.

Even for players whose US Open position is already secure, Cincinnati provides something equally valuable: matches against elite opposition. There is little substitute for facing one of the world’s best players shortly before a Grand Slam.

Fitness Will Be Closely Watched

Cincinnati will also offer important clues about injuries and fatigue. The professional tennis calendar leaves little recovery time during the summer. Players move from Europe to North America and then through a series of hard-court tournaments before reaching New York. Some arrive in Cincinnati searching for matches. Others arrive needing rest. Finding the balance is difficult.

A player eliminated early may lose an opportunity to build match rhythm before the US Open. A player who reaches the Cincinnati final could play through August 23 and then have only seven days before the first Sunday of singles competition in New York. That creates difficult decisions for players dealing with even relatively minor physical problems.

The withdrawal of defending men’s champion Carlos Alcaraz because of a wrist injury is a reminder of how quickly the complexion of the tournament can change at this point in the season. Others will arrive trying to manage their workloads while still pursuing one of the biggest titles available outside the Grand Slams.

What Cincinnati Can Tell Us

Tournament results alone will not predict the US Open. Tennis history is filled with players who struggled in their final warm-up tournament and then found their best form at a Grand Slam. Others have arrived in New York carrying a long winning streak only to lose early.

Still, several things will be worth watching in Cincinnati. How players move after long matches. Whether their first serves remain effective late in sets. How aggressively they return. Whether they can maintain their level through consecutive days of competition. And perhaps most importantly, how comfortable they look.

By the middle of August, there are few opportunities remaining to completely rebuild a game before the US Open. Cincinnati is where many of those questions begin to receive answers. The tournament’s qualifying rounds start August 11, with main-draw play beginning August 13 and the singles finals scheduled for August 23.

The US Open begins its Fan Week and qualifying activities the same day Cincinnati crowns its champions, before the main singles draws start August 30. For tennis fans here in Costa Rica and across Latin America, that makes Cincinnati much more than a warm-up event. It is the last major checkpoint before the tennis world turns its attention to New York.

World.title: OIJ Seizes Axolotls in Costa Rica Exotic Wildlife Investigation
World.content:
Costa Rican judicial agents arrested a 32-year-old man in Paso Ancho this week after raiding a home where investigators found several axolotls, turtles and equipment associated with keeping the animals. The operation was carried out by the Organismo de Investigación Judicial (OIJ) as part of an investigation into the suspected trafficking and commercial sale of wildlife. The suspect, identified by the surname Rosales, was taken into custody and transferred to the Prosecutor’s Office in Hatillo.

The investigation began in July after authorities received confidential information that wild animals were being offered for sale. Investigators suspect the animals were being sold or exchanged through electronic platforms. During the search of the Paso Ancho residence, agents seized several axolotls, turtles, chemical products and equipment used for keeping animals.

The axolotls immediately made the case unusual. The aquatic salamanders are native to Mexico and have become one of the world’s most recognizable exotic animals, helped by their unusual appearance, external feathery gills and growing presence in social media, toys and video games. Their popularity as pets stands in sharp contrast to their condition in nature.

The Mexican axolotl, Ambystoma mexicanum, is considered critically endangered in the wild. Its remaining natural habitat is centered around the canals and wetlands of Xochimilco in Mexico City, where pollution, urban growth, habitat degradation and invasive species have pushed the wild population toward extinction.

Axolotls are also listed under Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, or CITES, meaning international trade in the species is regulated. Large numbers of axolotls are bred in captivity around the world, however, making their presence in the pet trade much more common than their conservation status might suggest.

Authorities have not said whether the animals confiscated in Paso Ancho were captive-bred, how they entered Costa Rica or whether they were imported with any documentation. Those unanswered questions could become an important part of the investigation. Costa Rican wildlife rules cover more than animals native to Costa Rica. Exotic animals that are considered wildlife in their country of origin can also fall under Costa Rica’s wildlife regulations.

The rules place particularly tight restrictions on selling those animals as pets. Authorized facilities breeding exotic wildlife must meet registration and permit requirements, while the commercial sale of exotic wildlife as household pets is restricted. The Paso Ancho raid is also not the first time authorities have encountered axolotls in Costa Rica.

In July of last year, investigators seized two Mexican axolotls and 11 turtles during a raid on a business in Coronado. Because the axolotls could not be released in Costa Rica, the animals were eventually placed under the care of a wildlife sanctuary. The recurrence of axolotls in wildlife investigations highlights a less visible side of Costa Rica’s animal trade.

Costa Rica is internationally associated with protecting its own monkeys, sloths, macaws, sea turtles and other native wildlife, but authorities must also deal with foreign species arriving through an international exotic-pet market increasingly conducted online. Electronic marketplaces and social networks can make animals available far beyond their natural ranges while making it harder for buyers to determine where an animal came from, whether its importation was legal and whether the seller has authorization to trade it.

As of now, investigators have described Rosales as a suspect. No conviction has been entered, and prosecutors will determine what charges, if any, proceed. Authorities have also not disclosed the exact number of axolotls and turtles seized or announced where the confiscated animals will ultimately be housed.

World.title: Costa Rica Warns Pet Owners After Rabies Kills Cattle in Golfito
World.content:
A rabies outbreak that killed three cattle in southern Costa Rica has prompted renewed warnings for ranchers and pet owners to keep animals vaccinated, particularly in areas where vampire bats can transmit the virus. The latest outbreak was found in Pilón, in the area around Pavones, Golfito. The affected farm was placed under quarantine, and all 165 cattle on the property were ordered vaccinated as part of efforts to prevent further spread.

People who had direct contact with the infected animals are also receiving preventive treatment. The Golfito outbreak brings the number of reported paralytic bovine rabies outbreaks in Costa Rica to five so far in 2026. Cases have been recorded in Upala, Cañas, Osa and Golfito, reinforcing concern in rural areas where cattle and wildlife frequently come into contact.

The virus affecting cattle in these outbreaks is primarily transmitted by vampire bats, particularly Desmodus rotundus, a species that feeds on blood. Infected bats can bite the same animal repeatedly over several nights, allowing the virus to enter the animal’s body if it has not been vaccinated.

For cattle, rabies often appears differently than the aggressive form commonly associated with infected dogs. Bovine cases typically develop what is known as paralytic or “dumb” rabies. Early signs can include weakness in the rear legs, difficulty walking and problems remaining upright. As the disease advances, animals may develop paralysis of the tail and jaw, excessive salivation, difficulty swallowing and eventually become unable to stand.

The disease is fatal once it develops. The concern extends beyond cattle. Veterinary specialists are urging residents in affected and rabies-prone areas to make sure dogs and cats are current on their annual rabies vaccinations. Cats can face particular exposure because they sometimes hunt bats that enter homes, barns or nearby buildings. An unvaccinated dog or cat that contracts rabies can then expose people through bites, scratches or saliva.

Those in the area are also being warned not to handle bats, whether they appear healthy, injured or dead. Anyone bitten by a bat or who believes they may have had direct contact with one should seek medical attention immediately rather than waiting for symptoms to develop. Preventive treatment is most effective when started before the virus reaches the nervous system.

Costa Rica is home to a large diversity of bat species, and the current warning should not be seen as a reason to harm them. Most bats play important roles in the ecosystem by eating insects, spreading seeds and pollinating plants. The concern surrounding bovine rabies is focused primarily on blood-feeding vampire bats and the possibility of infected animals passing the virus to livestock or domestic animals.

Current control efforts emphasize vaccination rather than widespread killing of bats. Livestock in affected areas can be vaccinated, domestic animals kept current on their shots, and suspected cases reported quickly so veterinary teams can investigate. Ranchers are being told to watch cattle closely for neurological symptoms and to avoid handling animals showing unexplained paralysis, excessive salivation, coordination problems or sudden changes in behavior.

Suspected animals should not be moved, and carcasses should not be removed or handled without guidance from animal health personnel. The Golfito outbreak is particularly noteworthy in Costa Rica’s southern area, where cattle farms overlap with extensive forest and wildlife habitat.

Pavones is better known internationally for its beaches and surfing, but much of the surrounding canton remains rural, with farms, forests and small communities spread across a large area. There has been no indication that the outbreak poses a general threat to visitors traveling to Pavones or Golfito. The practical concern is direct contact with infected animals or bats, particularly for ranchers, veterinarians, farm workers and people living with unvaccinated pets in affected areas.

For most people the best protection is to keep dogs, cats and livestock vaccinated and report animals showing unusual neurological symptoms. This new warning comes as Costa Rica balances two important priorities: protecting livestock and public health while recognizing the ecological importance of bats in controlling insects, pollinating plants and dispersing seeds throughout Costa Rica’s ecosystems.

World.title: Two reportedly killed in fatal motorcycle collision on Mahogany Street
World.content:
Two reportedly killed in fatal motorcycle collision on Mahogany Street

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Breaking Belize News has received reports of a serious traffic accident involving motorcycles on Mahogany Street in Belize City during the early hours of Sunday morning.

Preliminary information indicates that the accident occurred at around 2:00 a.m. and involved at least two motorcycles. Images from the scene show multiple persons on the roadway as bystanders and other individuals gathered nearby.

World.title: Teen drowns in Belize River after bee swarm attack
World.content:
Teen drowns in Belize River after bee swarm attack

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A quiet walk along the Philip Goldson Highway turned to tragedy on Friday, August 7, 2026, when a 17-year-old girl drowned in the Belize River after she and her father were attacked by a swarm of bees near mile 7, sending the teen into deep water from which she never resurfaced.

The attack came at about 1:00 p.m., as the girl and her father, residents of Lord’s Bank who often walked that route together, passed a tree stump where the bees were nesting. The swarm descended on them both, and in the chaos that followed, as passersby rushed to assist her father, the teen went into the river, likely to escape the stings. That stretch of the river is said to be about 20 feet deep, and the girl, who could not swim, was unable to get back to the surface.

What followed was an hours-long search that drew together the Belize Coast Guard and eight civilian volunteers from 501 Lifeguard, who waded and dove through dark, murky water until about 3:30 p.m., when her body was finally recovered.

Tevin Conorquie, the 501 Lifeguard swimming instructor who first located her, described the ordeal, speaking to local media. “All we could have done was free dive and try to scan the area,” he said. “Due to the darkness of the water, it was intense for us to see but we still pulled through, we had the faith and the courage and we did what we had to do.” The team spent some three to four hours in the water, in conditions Conorquie called very difficult, “due to the fact that we know there may be crocodiles with us as well.”

When the teen’s brother arrived and the loss became real, the rescuers’ work turned from search to solace, the 501 Lifeguard team circling him in prayer. “With our team it’s just love,” said the organization’s owner, Andrew Gentle, noting that his instructors left their swimming classes to answer the call, and the whole team came.

The recovery weighed on the professionals too. “It’s never easy because you’re talking about the loss of life,” said Rear Admiral Gregory Soberanis, Commandant of the Belize Coast Guard, which responded to the request for dive operations. “There were times when I myself shed tears because of the situation. Especially when you’re talking about a young person such as the one today.”

The girl’s father is currently recovering in hospital. The family shared that the teen was living with autism and resided with her father. Officials have since sprayed the area where the bees were nesting.

Breaking Belize News extends its deepest condolences to the family, and its gratitude to the divers and volunteers who refused to leave the river without her.

World.title: The 80 million dollar question, a ledger for Belizeans to judge the BTL Speednet deal
World.content:
The 80 million dollar question, a ledger for Belizeans to judge the BTL Speednet deal

By Horace Palacio:

This week, the board of Belize Telemedia Limited approved spending 80 million dollars to buy Speednet, the company Belizeans know as Smart. It did so one day after the Chamber of Commerce publicly begged it to halt. The final agreement still must return to the board before signing, which means one thing.

There is still time for you to think. And you must, because this is not somebody else’s transaction.

BTL is majority owned by the Government of Belize, which is to say, by you. The Social Security Board, holding the retirement contributions of every working Belizean, owns another 34.2 percent. When BTL spends 80 million dollars, it is your company spending what is ultimately your money, with your pension fund along for the ride. You are the shareholder here. So today I will not hand you a verdict. I will hand you the ledger, both columns, honestly weighed, and then I will hand you the gavel.

First, the case for the deal, and let me make it properly, because it is not foolish.

Belize is a nation of 420,000 people carrying two complete, parallel telecommunications networks. Two sets of towers climbing the same skyline. Two fiber networks running down the same streets. Two billing systems, two headquarters, two of everything, serving a market smaller than a single foreign city. The case says this duplication is waste a small country cannot afford, and that one consolidated network could finally achieve the scale to modernize seriously, push fiber and coverage into the villages that neither company found profitable to serve, and strengthen reliability nationwide. BTL says the purchase needs no borrowing and not one new dollar from Social Security, paying for itself from Speednet’s own cash flows in roughly 4.2 years, with the profits of a unified telecom flowing to public hands instead of private ones. And there is a quieter argument some will weigh, that this deal ends Lord Ashcroft’s presence in Belizean telecommunications once and for all. That is the case for. Taken at face value, it is a vision of efficiency, inclusion, and sovereignty.

Now the other column, and it is heavy.

Start with what we already lived. Belizeans of a certain age remember the old single-provider era, and what it delivered, some of the region’s most expensive and slowest service, because a customer with nowhere to go is a customer who need not be pleased. Then competition arrived, and in the PUC’s own public comment file on this very deal sits a citizen pointing to the large price gap between BTL and Speednet as exactly what stands to be lost. Competition is not a theory in Belize. It is the reason your phone plan got better. This deal ends it.

Then the law. Section 42(4) of the Telecommunications Act prohibits agreements that significantly lessen competition in telecommunications. Buying your only major competitor is about the purest example imaginable. The Chamber adds a deeper alarm, Belize has no comprehensive competition or merger control legislation at all, no guardrails, meaning this would be a state-backed monopoly overseen only by a regulator, and the Chamber’s blunt warning is that regulation can never truly replace competition. Which raises the question no one has answered. When government owns the only telecom, and government appoints the referee, who exactly protects you?

Then the valuation. The financial model that justified the 80 million figure was prepared by Moore, a firm the unions say holds established ties to the BTL board, and it was paid for by BTL, the buyer, and reports indicate it stands among the only documents board members received. The unions call that a conflict of interest that renders the number inherently suspect, and demand what any buyer of a used car would demand, an independent inspection.

Then the arithmetic itself, because analysts who have studied the projections raise eyebrows at every line. The model reportedly projects Speednet earning a 66.5 percent profit margin, far above BTL’s own 44 percent, on revenue of 69 million dollars. Skeptics who place Speednet’s realistic revenue nearer 28 to 32 million calculate that the payback stretches not to 4.2 years but to somewhere between 13 and 25. The company’s own slides reportedly show combined revenue going flat, growing under one percent yearly once the deal closes, meaning the promised leap in profits rests almost entirely on cutting costs. And the seller’s own press release confirms where the knife lands, power, software, maintenance, and the duplicated departments, sales, marketing, human resources, finance, IT, purchasing. Behind every one of those words sit Belizean employees whose futures nobody has yet disclosed. BTL claims its payback is calculated on a discounted basis, yet the standard tools of any public investment of this size, the net present value, the internal rate of return, the formal schedules, have not been published for the shareholders, meaning you, to see.

Now count the voices, because the scorecard on this deal is unlike anything in recent memory. In favor, the BTL board and management. Urging halt or answers, the Chamber of Commerce speaking for over six thousand employers, the National Trade Union Congress speaking for organized labor, the parliamentary Opposition, and all four independent senators in a joint statement. Stop and appreciate the rarity. The employers and the unions of this country agree with each other about once a decade. They agree on this. When both the boss and the worker smell the same smoke, wise citizens check for fire.

So, Belize, was 80 million dollars for a national telecom monopoly worth it, or not? That verdict belongs to you. But hear me carefully, because this is the entire point of today’s column.

No honest verdict can be rendered on sealed evidence. Before any Belizean, for or against, can truly judge this deal, six things must be put on the table. Speednet’s audited financial statements for the past five years, so the revenue dispute dies on facts. A second, fully independent, internationally credible valuation, so the price stands on neutral ground. The full financial workings, published, so the payback claim can be tested by any accountant in the country. The honest scope of planned redundancies, so workers stop learning their futures from press releases. A public, rigorous PUC merger review under Section 42(4), conducted as law, not formality. And binding, enforceable consumer protections, in writing, before signing, not promises after.

If this deal is as good as its backers insist, none of that sunlight costs them anything. Good deals survive audits. Only bad ones fear them. And a transaction this size, by a publicly owned company, in a country still raw from the Mira Millions lesson about what happens in the dark, must be concluded in daylight or not at all.

The board has voted. The ink is not dry. You are the shareholder, Belize, all 420,000 of you.

Demand the books. Read the ledger. Then judge.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Jorge Messi, father and lifelong architect of Lionel’s career, dies at 68
World.content:
Jorge Messi, father and lifelong architect of Lionel’s career, dies at 68

By Breaking Belize News Staff ( HP): Jorge Messi, the father of Argentina captain Lionel Messi and the man who guided every step of the greatest career in football history, died Saturday at a hospital in Rosario, Argentina. He was 68.

Club Atlético Newell’s Old Boys, the Rosario club where both father and son once played in the youth ranks, announced his death, saying he had undergone treatment in recent months for an unspecified illness. The club described him as “the pillar and the person who, with vision, rigor and affection, supported the career of the best player of all time, alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini.”

The announcement casts the recent World Cup in a new and poignant light. After scoring against Algeria in Argentina’s opening match, Messi was visibly emotional, later saying he wept for “a reason unrelated to sports” and that he had endured “difficult, complicated days.” Media speculation at the time drew a sharp statement from the Messi family confirming that Jorge was experiencing a health issue, while insisting that “a person’s health and the peace of mind of their loved ones should not be the subject of speculation.” Messi went on to captain Argentina to the final, where they finished runners-up to Spain, before returning home to rest.

A chemical technician and former steelworker, Jorge Messi played as a midfielder in Newell’s youth system before military service ended his own football path. His life’s work became his son’s. He traveled with a young Lionel to Barcelona in the early 2000s for the trial that opened La Masia’s doors, negotiated the contracts with Barcelona and the later moves to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami, and managed his son’s business affairs throughout.

Lionel Messi himself once described what those early days cost them both. “Sometimes I would lock myself in my room to cry when we arrived in Barcelona, or my dad would do the same without me seeing him,” he said in 2007. “My dad even asked me what I wanted to do when we were feeling down, if I wanted to stay or go back, and I wanted to stay, and he stayed with me.”

Tributes flowed Saturday. CONMEBOL offered condolences “with respect and affection for Lionel,” and Argentine federation president Claudio Tapia honoured Jorge “for having raised a person of values: humble, respectful, and deeply committed to others.” The federation ordered a moment of silence at all matches across every category of Argentine football, with players, referees and coaching staff to wear black armbands.

Jorge Messi is survived by his wife Celia and their children. Breaking Belize News extends condolences to the Messi family.

World.title: BDF and University of Belize deepen partnership on education and training
World.content:
BDF and University of Belize deepen partnership on education and training

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Belize Defence Force and the University of Belize are strengthening their collaboration, with the BDF’s Training and Doctrine Directorate visiting the university to meet with President and members of his staff on furthering joint efforts between the Ministry of Defence and Border Security and the nation’s leading academic institution.

The engagement provided an opportunity for discussions on ongoing programs, future initiatives, and the continued growth of the partnership between the two institutions, according to the BDF.

Members of the Force also attended the closing ceremony of the Digital Literacy Program hosted by the University of Belize, a program in which the BDF proudly participated. The Force described the training as another important step in equipping its members with valuable knowledge and skills for both professional and personal development.

With the university preparing for the upcoming academic year, plans were established to continue and expand engagements between both institutions.

The BDF said it remains committed to promoting higher learning, professional development and continuous education as essential components in transforming training and developing a more capable and knowledgeable Force, summing up the effort in its own words: investing in education, strengthening our Force, serving Belize.

World.title: Black Orchid Resort gives locals 20 percent off all rooms through October 1
World.content:
Black Orchid Resort gives locals 20 percent off all rooms through October 1

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP):Belizeans looking for a getaway without the border run have a fresh reason to look toward Burrell Boom. Black Orchid Resort has launched its River Wild Escape locals special, offering 20 percent off all rooms for Belizean residents from August 1 to October 1.

The discount applies across the resort’s full range of accommodations: Garden View Rooms, River View Rooms, Garden View Suites and Riverfront Suites, so everything from a simple couple’s night away to a riverfront splurge qualifies.

The two month window conveniently covers the September celebrations, making the special a natural fit for a patriotic long weekend on the river.

Bookings can be made at 610-0912 or by email at [email protected]. Escape, relax, and experience the wild side of Belize, at local prices.

World.title: Belize @45 Workshop Explores Sovereignty and Nationhood
World.content:
Belize @45 Workshop Explores Sovereignty and Nationhood

By Zoila Palma: The Belize @45 Workshop, a three-day professional development training, was held from August 5 to 7, 2026, bringing together educators from across the country to examine what Belize’s independence really means.

The training was a collaborative effort of the Institute for Social and Cultural Research (ISCR), the Belize Archives and Records Service (BARS), the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science & Technology (MOECST), specifically Ms. Ruby Reyes of the Belizean Studies Curriculum and Assessment Unit, the George Price Centre for Peace and Development, the University of Belize, and Galen University.

During the training, historian and diplomat Assad Shoman challenged educators to reflect on the “role of teachers and students in shaping Belize’s future.”

The event included virtual sessions and an in-person learning session at the George Price Centre for Peace and Development in Belmopan, equipping educators with new tools and perspectives to bring Belize’s history and independence journey to life for students.

Organizers emphasized that Belize’s independence is not simply an achievement of the past, but an ongoing process, underscoring the message: “Independence is the beginning!

World.title: Belizeans Travel Across U.S. for Passport and Nationality Services at Evanston Diaspora Hub
World.content:
Belizeans Travel Across U.S. for Passport and Nationality Services at Evanston Diaspora Hub

By Zoila Palma: Belizeans from across the Chicago area and several other parts of the United States travelled to Evanston this weekend to access passport and nationality services brought directly to the diaspora by Belize’s Ministry of Immigration, Governance and Labour.

The three-day Evanston Diaspora Hub runs from August 7 to 9. The event provides passport and nationality services, including first-time and renewal passport applications, as well as applications for Belizean nationality by descent.

The ministry says that the outreach provides a more convenient way to complete important documentation without having to travel to Belize. Belizean passport applicants are required to appear in person at an Immigration Office in Belize or at a designated Belizean diplomatic or consular mission, making mobile outreach efforts particularly valuable for Belizeans living far from those locations.

The Evanston hub also highlighted the strong community ties among Belizeans living in the United States. Some Chicago-area residents noted that they have built a vibrant Belizean community and are preparing to host a fundraiser on Saturday to provide scholarships to 14 Belizean-American students attending school.

Belize’s Ambassador to the United States, H.E. Nestor E. Mendez, visited the hub alongside Belize’s Ambassador for Diaspora Relations, Sandhya Murphy, as officials engaged with Belizeans accessing the services.

The Evanston initiative follows other diaspora outreach efforts by the Government of Belize in the United States. Earlier this year, approximately 230 passports and 17 nationality certificates were delivered to Belizeans abroad during another outreach initiative, reflecting continued demand for documentation services within Belizean communities across the United States.

World.title: Bravery born of pain
World.content:
HIGGINS...I will do whatever I can to protect the kids of our society

FUELLED by her own childhood experiences with sexual assault and incidents of incest that she’d witnessed, Susan Higgins helped track down Troy Ellis, the man accused of the rape and murder of eight-year-old Talia Thompson in Discovery Bay, St Ann, in 2023.

Just shy of three years later, her actions have earned her national recognition. Higgins is among four Jamaicans slated to receive the Badge of Honour for Gallantry at this year’s national honours and awards ceremony scheduled for October.

Ellis, while receiving treatment at hospital under police guard following Talia’s death in September 2023, reportedly escaped. But Higgins later encountered him on the road and played a key role in getting him back into police custody.

For the 50-year-old, the national recognition is deeply personal.

“I feel happy and blessed to know that I can be a help to the helpless and a voice of the voiceless,” she told the

Jamaica Observer.

“When I opened the paper [last Thursday] and I saw Susan Higgins, mi dear! It was 140 people and fi mi name in there, me seh! No man, me feel good,” she added, erupting in laughter.

Talia was allegedly raped and murdered on September 23, 2023. Ellis, who was reportedly known to the family, was subsequently taken to hospital after allegedly injuring himself.

When Higgins heard that he had escaped from police custody, she said she immediately felt a sense of urgency to do something.

She said she was on her way home and her daughter was with her. When they got to the vicinity of the Firearm Licensing Authority office in Discovery Bay, she noticed a man attempting to conceal his face when the motor vehicle headlights illuminated him.

She said she immediately became suspicious and asked the driver to turn the vehicle around.

When they approached the man, Higgins said she began questioning him about his injury, deliberately remaining calm and acting as though she was simply curious about why he was on the road so late. She recalled Ellis telling her that he had recently been discharged from hospital.

Higgins said she continued to speak with him through the window of the vehicle while it drove slowly beside him, at the same time her daughter was conducting a quick online search. The search, she said, confirmed that the man she was speaking to matched the description of the escapee.

“I told him to pull up his shirt to let me see his wound. I was just playing slick because I wanted to see if he had a gun on him. When I saw that he didn’t have a gun, I asked him where he was going, and he said ‘Portland Road’,” she recalled.

“I said, ‘Do you need a ride?’ And he said, ‘Yes,’ not knowing it was the police me a carry him to. I said, ‘All right, when you reach your destination you tell me.’ During the ride, he was talking so intelligently to me. He didn’t show any sign of [being of] unsound mind, so I talked to him and talked to him until he said, ‘Me a come off here so.’ When he said that, me dumb, deaf, and blind, and stopped talking. I took him straight to Discovery Bay police,” said Higgins.

When they arrived, Higgins said the station’s door was closed, so she instructed her daughter to knock.

A cop came outside and Higgins said the driver immediately announced that they had found the man wanted in connection with Talia’s death. At that point, Higgins said Ellis became aware that he had been identified and attempted to resist.

She said she struggled to restrain him before eventually getting him into the police station, after which his identity was confirmed and he was returned to police custody.

For Higgins, the decision to intervene was not about recognition or praise, it was about doing what she would hope someone else would do if her child was in danger.

“Too many times children are being murdered, raped, left abandoned. As a woman, I didn’t get the love and the care of a parent. I actually grew up in the wild because my parents gave me away to a family, and [a man] attempted to rape me. It made me so aggressive, and I said if anybody ever do this to any pickney, if me catch them, me a go unalive them, but I did my best that night to not do what I wanted to because my little daughter was there and I couldn’t bear to do it,” she told the Sunday Observer.

“So many kids get raped and murdered, and so many of these cases go unanswered. I said, I am going to stand up and be a voice for the voiceless and a help for the helpless,” said Higgins.

“I will do whatever I can to protect the kids of our society,” she said. “I didn’t know the parents or the grandparents of that child, but I feel elated that I can help a mother to get some form of justice,” said Higgins.

“As I go along, I will always try to help somebody. My living will not be in vain,” she declared.

World.title: Running dry
World.content:
Paul Williams rinses a vehicle moments after it exited a drive-through car wash. (Photos: Naphtali Junior)

FACING the annual prospect of cutting staff or paying to truck untreated water just to keep their businesses afloat, car wash operators across Kingston and St Andrew say they are once again bracing for a difficult period as stricter restrictions loom.

Several operators told the Jamaica Observer they fear they may be forced to temporarily shutter their operation or find alternatives to clean vehicles if the drought persists, though many remain hopeful that rainfall will ease the situation before the restrictions intensify.

Last week, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda warned that full prohibition orders on the use of potable water are possible by August 10, if weather conditions remain unchanged or worsen.

Samuda made the announcement after the Meteorological Service of Jamaica projected prolonged dry conditions stretching into October this year.

Under a prohibition order issued by the National Water Commission (NWC), the use of treated water for non-essential activities is banned during periods of severe drought. Prohibited activities include watering gardens, lawns and farms; refilling tanks, ponds and swimming pools; and washing vehicles with a hose. Breaches may result in a fine or imprisonment for up to 30 days.

Speaking at a Jamaica Observer Press Club earlier this year, Samuda said efforts are under way to strengthen the country’s water infrastructure, so Jamaica can avoid imposing similar restrictions during future dry spells. However, until then, restrictions will be in place.

David Chambers, manager of an auto spa, said he has worked in the industry for 30 years and is no stranger to water restrictions, describing them as one of the inevitable challenges the business faces whenever drought conditions arise.

He said the business typically copes by purchasing untreated water sourced from rivers. While the additional expense of trucking water significantly increases operating costs, Chambers said the auto spa absorbs the cost rather than passing it on to customers, fearing higher prices could drive away business.

“People have to still eat food, and the workmen have their families to feed, so it’s not a situation where we can just shut down the car wash. We have to find ways and means to operate,” he told the Sunday Observer.

He said that if trucked water is no longer available, he may have no choice but to close his business, a decision he would make with a heavy heart because of its impact on his employees. However, he said he is researching alternatives.

Chambers said he discovered waterless car-washing products that could allow the business to continue operating, but the specialised chemicals would have to be imported and come at a high cost, making the option difficult to sustain.

“Right now we are in a situation where we have to just watch and see what is happening more than anything else… We are praying for some rain because with rain we know that the water situation will go away because the [catchment] areas will have water, so that will be good for us,” said Chambers.

The cry for rain is also being made by Paul Williams, team leader at One Wash, a drive-thru car wash in the Corporate Area. Williams said currently, One Wash has three water drums on the premises which cost about $18,000 to refill. That will allow them to wash up to 20 cars.

“It affects us a lot, so we have to just try to wash off the cars fast. Luckily, the machine we use recycles water. We have a drum on the inside where it recycles, but for the machines that we use to rinse off the cars, we use the drum, and that takes water, so we try not to waste it,” said Williams.

“If it gets worse, we have to close until the water situation gets better. I’m not prepared for that. I have to go home and sit down and have no work. I don’t know how I am going to manage. I hope rain falls so we don’t have any more water restrictions because right now, I don’t have any water at my house. I got up this morning, and no water, and it’s going on two months now,” he told the Sunday Observer.

Williams appealed for improvement in Jamaica’s water resilience to ensure that businesses that rely on the supply do not have to close their doors.

“We need to find a fix. It cannot be that every year we have to lose business,” he argued.

Chenell Allison, a supervisor at Ten-O-Let Car and Carpet Care, said the company is often forced to make staff changes.

“We try to cut where we can, so maybe staff that is on weekly we give them fewer days,” Allison explained.

She added the company also has contractual workers who get paid per car, so it is less burdensome when business is slow and restrictions are in place.

Allison noted that the company currently trucks water to fill two tanks to stay afloat, but it cannot afford to do so for an extended period.

“If our budgeted amount for purchasing is exceeding profits, then we have a problem, but we are not there yet. We are used to it. It hasn’t come to that yet, so hopefully we can get some rain before it does and we have to shut down,” said Allison.

Another car wash operator said he does not believe it would be worth continuing the business if the drought worsens. He said he is prepared to conserve, because he has other businesses that are more profitable and do not require water usage.

He, too, called for measures to protect water-reliant businesses during a drought.

Samuda said the Government has several major projects under way aimed at making Jamaica more resilient during periods of drought. Among them is the Rio Cobre Water Treatment Plant, now under construction in Content, St Catherine, which he described as a game-changing investment.

The facility will treat raw water from Rio Cobre and inject 15 million gallons of potable water into the NWC’s distribution network each day, supplying more than 150,000 customers across St Catherine, Kingston and St Andrew. The project remains on track for completion in May 2027.

He said the Rio Cobre development forms part of a broader national strategy to strengthen Jamaica’s water infrastructure rather than relying on emergency measures whenever drought conditions arise. According to Samuda, investments made since 2015 have significantly improved water efficiency in Kingston, St Andrew and Portmore by reducing leakage across the network from 71 per cent to 37 per cent. As a result, the system now loses approximately 12 million fewer gallons of water per day than it did in 2015.

In addition, work is progressing on the Western Water Resilience Programme, while plans are advancing to construct new treatment plants and expand water catchment systems, including the Hermitage Dam.

Expanding water catchment capacity is one solution that motorist Miguel Brown believes could help Jamaica better withstand future droughts. Brown, who regularly uses a car wash to maintain his vehicle, argued that the island has ample underutilised land that could be used to capture and store rainwater for use during dry periods.

“We have a lot of springs, we have a lot of rivers, we just need somewhere for the water to stay so we don’t have the problem every year,” he reasoned.

He noted that he washes his car twice a month but is willing to cut down to once a month to help conserve.

“All of us know that we have to save in a crisis like this; in the dry season, we have to save. Once everybody has the understanding and sees what is happening — the entire Jamaica should see what is happening in the dry times and we must get used to it by now,” said Brown.

Conrad Malcolm washes his car once per week. He said he is prepared to clean his car himself using recycled water from home or seek out car wash operators who have access to untreated water and are prepared for the drought.

He urged greater investment in water storage facilities, given the increase in the number of households.

“We have more households coming up and each household will use more water. We need to invest in more water facilities. There are rivers; we have the sea; we can treat the water. We can do much better to alleviate the problem rather than every year we are at the same place,” he stressed.

World.title: Plie’s AMALGAMATION Gala set for 10th anniversary finale in Jamaica
World.content:
Plie Collective .

Jamaica is set for an electrifying celebration of dance excellence as Plie’s AMALGAMATION Gala returns to the Little Theatre on August 29 and 30.

Marking the 10th anniversary of Plié for The Arts, this milestone edition promises to be its most spectacular staging yet.

Held under the distinguished patronage of Misty Copeland, AMALGAMATION Gala 2026 will close its Caribbean tour in Jamaica after performances in Trinidad and Tobago and Barbados.

This year’s gala will honour Desmond Richardson, the iconic American dancer, choreographer, co-founder and co-artistic director of Complexions Contemporary Ballet.

The full company will headline the programme, bringing the Caribbean première of Dwight Rhoden’s show-stopping Love Rocks, set to music by Lenny Kravitz, along with Rhoden’s other breathtaking works Ave Maria and Mercy.

Audiences will also see New York City Ballet’s Christopher Grant in a duet with the stunning Ashley Green of Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater. The ever-spectacular Caught by Parsons Dance, as well as Suite Etta, a stunning piece performed by Adji Cissoko, recently named associate artistic director, and her electrifying dance partner, Shuaib Elhassan from Alonzo King LINES Ballet.

Adding to the excitement, the Plié Caribbean Collective, now featuring exceptional dancers from across the region, will share the stage with these international stars. The Collective will perform powerful works from its repertoire with the Caribbean première of On the Verge of Ascending, created by Swedish choreographer Jon Ole Olstad and Carmina Burano choreographed by Ilya Jivoy delivering a true fusion of Caribbean talent and global brilliance.

At the heart of AMALGAMATION is a bold vision of bringing the best of the world together with the best of the region.

Beyond the stage, the gala creates opportunities for training and artistic exchange through workshops and masterclasses led by participating global companies. As part of the celebration, Complexions Contemporary Ballet will host free masterclasses, with outstanding participants eligible for immersive scholarship opportunities with the company.

With a different experience offered each night, AMALGAMATION has grown into a regional destination event with global ambition. Founder and Artistic Director Marisa Benain says the gala is built to stand among the world’s best: “The Amalgamation Gala offers audiences a programme and an experience that is hard to match anywhere in the world. We have what it takes to produce a dance gala at an international standard, and our aim is always to make each Amalgamation Gala more spectacular than the last.”

World.title: Jamaica leads Caribbean in Airbnb emergency housing
World.content:
This house in Parottee, St Elizabeth, crumbled during Hurricane Melissa.

MORE than two-thirds of the 1,500 nights of emergency housing provided for families displaced by natural disasters across the Caribbean by Airbnb.org since 2020 have been utilised in Jamaica.

Christoph Gorder, executive director of Airbnb.org — the independent non-profit founded by Airbnb to provide emergency housing in times of crisis — puts the figure at more than 1,000 nights.

“The vast majority of that housing was provided in the wake of Hurricane Melissa, reflecting the scale of the storm’s impact,“ Gorder said in an e-mailed response to the Jamaica Observer.

He said the non-profit is proud of the role its community has played in supporting people in Jamaica during emergencies.

“And as our partnership with the Caribbean Disaster Emergency Management Agency (CDEMA) and other partners like IOM, Church World Services, and All Hands and Hearts demonstrates, we stand ready to help in the future,” Gorder said.

Last month, Airbnb and Airbnb.org signed an agreement with CDEMA to accelerate access to temporary housing for disaster victims across the agency’s 20 Caribbean member countries. The agreement is designed to help mobilise available housing support after a disaster, helping close temporary housing gaps that often emerge in the immediate aftermath of a crisis.

The partnership is anchored by a memorandum of understanding (MOU) that addresses roles, coordination, and activations during the critical early days of a disaster response. CDEMA will help coordinate with local responders to identify people with emergency housing needs, while Airbnb.org will support these efforts by helping provide free, available emergency housing.

Airbnb.org leverages the Airbnb platform to help connect people who need a place to stay with listings on the platform, enabling guests to book homes that meet their needs, including kitchens, laundry rooms, and pet-friendly spaces. All stays are offered at no cost to guests and funded by Airbnb.org.

According to CDEMA’s Executive Director Elizabeth Riley, the partnership represents a valuable addition to the region’s disaster preparedness and response framework.

“As we enter the 2026 hurricane season, the MOU strengthens our ability to support people affected by disasters through innovative solutions and enhanced regional collaboration. By combining CDEMA’s regional coordination capacity with Airbnb.org’s emergency housing support, we are expanding the resources available to communities when they need them most,” Riley said. “It also reflects a shared commitment to ensuring that affected populations can access timely assistance and recover more quickly following disasters.”

Additionally, Airbnb, in collaboration with CDEMA and the Caribbean Tourism Organization (CTO), launched a hurricane safety guide to support communities and educate the public about what to do before, during, and after a hurricane. It also includes emergency contact information for multiple Caribbean islands. Airbnb said it will provide the hurricane safety guide to hosts in the region so they can share with their guests.

“Safety in the Caribbean is a top priority for Airbnb. By collaborating with expert organisations like CDEMA and the CTO, we are ensuring our hosts and guests have access to vital, locally sourced resources to prepare for and navigate hurricane season,” said Carlos Muñoz, Airbnb’s director of public policy for the Caribbean and Central America.

World.title: SALMON FINDS A WAY
World.content:
Jamaica’s Joseph Salmon competes in the men’s discus throw qualification at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon, on Saturday. Salmon qualified for today’s final with a mark of 62.10m. (Photo: Paul A Reid)

OREGON, USA — Inspired by his teammate Michael Andre Edwards’ last-round heroics in the men’s triple jump final on Friday evening, world leader Joseph Salmon pulled off a similar nervy feat on Saturday to qualify for today’s men’s discus throw final on the final day of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships here at Hayward Field.

After two fouls and on the brink of failing to qualify, Salmon threw 62.10m on his final attempt in Group B, qualifying to join Kamari Kennedy who had qualified in the first group with 60.65m. Both surpassed the automatic qualifying mark of 60.50m.

Meanwhile, Jamaica will hope to defend both 4x100m relay titles today after qualifying on Saturday.

All four Jamaican relay teams, including the two 4x400m teams, advanced to their finals.

On Friday, Edwards pulled off a final-round miracle to win the men’s triple jump, and Salmon said although he was not expecting to need all three qualifying attempts, he was inspired by what he saw.

“I am really confident. What Michael did [Friday], he gave me a boost, gave me a boost, man so we’ll see. It’s going to be a show [Sunday],” he said after qualifying.

Salmon fouled his first two attempts, saying his technique was not the best, while his second attempt was ruled a foul for stepping over the board.

“In the third round I got everything together and just sent it out there,” he said, adding that he was not thinking about any particular distance but was simply focused on qualifying. “I am pleased to say I’m not really throwing at my full potential but just to get into the final.”

Kennedy was delighted with his third throw, which was over the qualifying mark.

“I was really happy. I’m glad that I got the qualifying mark and so now I can prepare for the finals,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

Kennedy had failed to advance from the first round of the shot put earlier in the championships but said the discus qualification made up for that disappointment.

Strong legs from lead-off runner Kyle Bodden and anchor Sanjay Seymore helped the Jamaican men’s team win their heat of the 4x100m in 39.51 seconds.

Nyrone Wade, who was part of the team that won in Lima, Peru, two years ago, and Nathaniel Martin were also part of the team that beat Japan, which finished second in 39.65 seconds, and Hong Kong, which set a national Under-20 record of 39.66.

The women’s team of Samoya Brown, Theianna Lee Terrelonge, Natrece East and Renecia Edwards finished second in their heat in 43.61 seconds, behind Australia which ran a national Under-20 record 43.44. Nigeria was third in 43.65.

East told the Sunday Observer that the team was happy to advance to the final.

“I think we performed well. I mean, it’s the first three that advance to the finals so we did enough to make it to the finals. And, I feel like when we run in the finals we can do better,” she said.

East said they were going after medals and, while admitting the baton exchanges were good, hoped they could be better today.

“Yeah, I feel like they were good. I mean, there’s always room for improvement so in the final we have to make even better changes and we will be good.”

Earlier, the team of Daniellia Dixon, Kristen Herbert, Davine Dickenson and Shanika Lindsay finished third in the women’s 4x400m, qualifying in 3:35.93 behind Germany, which won in 3:34.35, and Slovenia, which ran a national Under-20 record 3:35.60.

The men’s team of Nishawn Walker, Jordan Rehedul, Jaeden Campbell and Jabulani McLeod also placed third in their semi-final heat in 3:06.44. The USA led with a World Under-20-leading 3:04.55 while South Africa was second in 3:05.08, with both teams being gold-medal prospects.

World.title: COCKTAILS With…
World.content:
(Photo: Marz Jackson)

ANNALISA “@annaixe” GUTHRIE

Designer | Creative Practitioner

We’re stirring things up.

The Style Observer serves up Cocktails With with a twist.

For Independence 64, designer Annalisa Guthrie is toasting the icons, influences, and cultural greats who helped shape Jamaica — and, in turn, shaped the woman she is today.

Known for her knack of transforming the most unexpected materials into high-fashion statements, Guthrie is turning heritage into a silhouette, history into a statement, and Jamaican pride into something wearable.

Style Observer: What was the inspiration behind the new looks?

Annalisa Guthrie: “Our greatness today is a result of who we have been and who we continue to be. Here’s my way of celebrating the greats who helped shape the culture; the same culture that has made me who I am and what I’ll always be proud to be — Jamaican,” she shared.

SO shares the three-piece collection.

Asymmetrical Mesh Merino Dress

A staple in Jamaican fashion is the mesh marino, most commonly worn in the context of streetwear, and which has been styled in many ways, especially by male reggae artistes. I thought it would be interesting to make something of a gown out of different cut-up pieces of several merinos, but in a very raw and rugged way to keep in line with the tradition of “tun yuh hand and mek fashion”. I didn’t want this piece to feel as refined, but I still wanted it to feel flattering and unique and fashionable for the female form while still being raw.

Dancehall Queen 2.0

Nineties dancehall fashion has always been the blueprint for so many internationally, and I thought it was very important to pay tribute to not only original Dancehall Queen Carlene and some of her iconic golden looks, but also to pay homage to Spice, the queen of dancehall. The bejewelled bra has diamond shapes that meet the eye immediately, but If you look closely at the end of the chains you can see symbols (clubs, hearts and spades) to represent the symbols in a card pack — a nuanced way to honour Spice as “queen inna di deck”.

Bandana

For far too long I’ve heard criticism about the Bandana being outdated or not seen as beautiful, despite it being our national dress. I think it is our responsibility as artists to create and help others view things through a different lens. I made this video originally for the purpose of reimagining the Bandana print in a way that felt reverent, but modern. It was meant to be the main attraction. Jamaican folklorist Louise Bennett-Coverley championed for our cultural pride in a way that inspired me deeply and she wore the bandana proudly. I wanted to honour her by carrying the torch and using my creativity to represent her national pride in present day. I hope people are able to feel her spirit and reignite their own love for this little island when seeing this piece take form.

CREDITS

Visuals: Marz Jackson, @marz_jackson
