World.title: Carlton close on stunning AFL top 10 finish; Rowell dominant as Suns snap streak; Blues hold sway in AFLW opener
World.content:
A nightmare and an unlikely fairytale played out in unison at Marvel Stadium in a rare Sunday night game.

Carlton continued their revival under interim coach Josh Fraser and took a major step towards qualifying for the AFL’s inaugural wildcard round with a 44-point triumph over St Kilda, who played without Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera for all bar the first nine minutes.

The Blues had a single win from nine matches when Michael Voss resigned as coach in May, but this was their 10th victory in 12 games since Fraser took over – and propels them two games clear of the injury-ravaged Saints.

No good: Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera on the bench after his hamstring injury. AFL Photos via Getty Images

Tenth-placed Carlton can lock in a wildcard berth if they defeat the Western Bulldogs next Sunday, strengthening Fraser’s chances of being Voss’ permanent replacement.

St Kilda mustered only eight goals and 62 points in total, marking the eighth time in Fraser’s tenure that the suddenly stingy Blues conceded fewer than 80 points as they again dominated uncontested possession.

Playing for his third club, Francis Evans produced arguably a career-best performance with 22 disposals, 12 inside 50s, 10 score involvements and a goal to headline Carlton’s performance.

George Hewett had 20 of his 26 disposals by half-time, when the Blues already led by 25 points, while Marc Pittonet (two goals) took the ruck honours over ex-teammate Tom De Koning and Rowan Marshall.

The Saints, in 11th, remain mathematically in the race with a fortnight to go in the home-and-away season. But Ross Lyon’s men resembled the walking wounded on a night they honoured the late Danny Frawley in the sixth annual Spud’s Game.

Wanganeen-Milera barely trained all week because of a hip issue, but hobbled from the ground early in the first quarter after suffering a left hamstring injury in a chase on the wing.

St Kilda ruled out their $2 million match-winner soon after, and his season is probably also over.

They must beat Richmond and Gold Coast in the last two rounds to keep their finals chances alive – but also need the Bulldogs and Carlton to stumble in both their remaining clashes.

World.title: VietJet to offer international flights from Western Sydney
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessCompaniesAviation VietJet to offer international flights from Western Sydney Chris Zappone August 10, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Vietnam-based low-cost carrier VietJet is set to become the third international airline offering flights from Western Sydney International airport, with an announcement expected as soon as Monday to confirm planned services likely to begin with flights to Ho Chi Minh City. The airport and the airline are likely to formalise VietJet’s entry to Australia’s newest international airport to meet growing demand for Australian travel to Asia and cater to diverse communities in Western Sydney, industry sources told this masthead. VietJet is expanding rapidly, and likely to fly between Ho Chi Minh City and Western Sydney. Paul Rovere VietJet will begin offering two weekly return flights between Western Sydney and Ho Chi Minh City from January, stepping up three weekly return flights from March, said sources with knowledge of the deal. Full details will be released on Monday. VietJet may also provide an update on the prospects of a launch of domestic services in Australia in what would be a major boost to competition in a market dominated by Qantas Group and Virgin, as Vietnam’s President To Lam embarks on a state visit to Australia and New Zealand this week.



Related Article Aviation Flying into night sky, first cargo plane from Sydney’s new airport sparks parcel frenzy The budget airline has already requested the 2252 take-off and landing slots from the slot coordinator for Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport. Industry sources say that even if VietJet plans to initially fly between Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane, the airline would still be months away from offering its first flights. To date, Western Sydney Airport has secured international flights from Air New Zealand, to launch in October, and Singapore Airlines to launch in November, as well as Qantas and Jetstar, which will begin in October. VietJet and the Western Sydney Airport were contacted for comment. The low-cost carrier operates daily return flights to Ho Chi Minh City, formerly known as Saigon, from both Sydney Airport and Melbourne, offering seven weekly services for each city. It also offers five weekly return flights between Brisbane and Ho Chi Minh City, as well as three weekly flights between Perth and Ho Chi Minh City. Basing flights from Western Sydney International Airport could appeal to historically Vietnamese communities in south-western Sydney suburbs such as Cabramatta, Canley Vale and Canley Heights.



VietJet’s website currently allows searches for flights between Ho Chi Minh City and Western Sydney International, although none are offered yet. VietJet is in expansion mode across the region with subsidiaries in Thailand and the Central Asian nation of Kazakhstan. Headquartered in Hanoi, the airline has 107 planes primarily based in the Vietnamese cities of Ho Chi Minh City, Da Nang, Cam Ranh and Hai Phong. It has placed orders for 100 A321neos and another 20 A330neos. In total, the airline has planned orders to receive more than 600 Airbus and Boeing aircraft over the next decade. It also has plans to lease 10 Chinese COMAC-made C909s. In June 2025, in announcing the new Airbus order, Vietjet chairwoman Nguyen Thi Phuong Thao said she had a “vision and the determination to make Vietnam a regional aviation hub for passenger transportation, technical services, logistics, training, research, global supply chains, and aviation infrastructure”.



It has 40 wide body aircraft on order. Vietnam has become a popular vacation destination for Australians with flight capacity between the two countries rising to 263 per cent of pre-COVID levels in April of last year, according to Corporate Traveller, a division of Flight Centre Travel Group. World.title: Free GP visits on the rise as 1400 clinics ditch out-of-pocket fees
World.content:
PoliticsFederalMedicare Free GP visits on the rise as 1400 clinics ditch out-of-pocket fees Michelle Griffin August 10, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bulk-billing rates continue to climb on the back of the Albanese government’s multibillion-dollar signature Medicare incentive, as the latest health department data shows increases in the number of free consultations for patients in all states and territories. The national bulk-billing rate for the June 2026 quarter rose to 84.1 per cent, almost 4 percentage points higher than in the same quarter last year. Almost four out of five patients aged 16 to 64 had their doctor’s appointment bulk billed in the June quarter – an increase of 8.2 percentage points year on year. Bulk billing for consultations with the elderly, which are typically more complex and lengthy, has lagged.



The strong results reinforce the record 7 percentage point rise in the take-up of bulk billing by GPs since November 2025, when the Albanese government began paying incentives to doctors not to charge out-of-pocket fees. The fastest take-up was in the Northern Territory, up 13 percentage points in the June quarter to 90.8 per cent. Almost nine in 10 patient visits in NSW and Victoria were bulk billed in the same quarter, 87.5 per cent and 85.7 per cent respectively. Bulk billing for older patients, who often have more complex needs and require longer with their doctor, is lagging. Virginia Star The laggard is the Australian Capital Territory, where only 59.3 per cent of visits in the last quarter were bulk billed, up 2.4 percentage points. A wealthier enclave than other states and territories, the nation’s capital has trouble recruiting doctors to meet a local shortage and does not meet the criteria for the regional incentives to attract GPs. More than 1400 practices have switched from mixed billing to bulk billing since the incentives were introduced, according to the federal health department.



The steady increase means Labor is on track to meet its $8.5 billion pledge ahead of the 2025 election to make nine of 10 GP visits free by 2030. Many GP clinics had previously restricted bulk billing to children and concession-card holders, but the new incentives give doctors extra payments if they waive out-of-pocket fees. For a standard consult by doctors in metropolitan areas that is about $63.50. Clinics that bulk bill all their patients receive an extra quarterly payment set at 12.5 per cent of the practice’s Medicare billing. Opposition health spokeswoman Anne Ruston claimed during June’s Senate estimates that some Labor MPs had bullied clinics into signing up for bulk billing.



She said MPs were “putting pressure on a practice by expressing great disappointment that they’re not bulk billing, when the department’s own figures suggest that 30 per cent of practices would be worse off if they went to a full bulk-billing model”. “You’ve got your MPs out there making these comments, trying to bully, as I say, their local GPs.” Related Article Exclusive

IVF Rose had two heartbreaking IVF losses. Then her specialist clocked one crucial detail A Senate estimates hearing was told by health department officials that their modelling showed 4800 practices out of 6600 studied would be better off if they shifted to bulk billing with the new incentives – meaning 27 per cent of practices would not be better off. Dr Michael Wright, president of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, said that while the incentives helped doctors bulk bill, they did not cover the costs for many practices – “even the government’s own modelling [indicates] it was never going to cover the costs for all practices”.



“General practices are small businesses, you know,” Wright said. “No one wins if practices close their doors because they can’t afford to keep their doors open. If politicians really want to help people all around Australia have affordable access to general practice care, the best way to do that is by increasing Medicare rebates, particularly for the longer and more complex consultations, because that’s the care that GPs are increasingly providing for our patients. But the way Medicare is structured, there’s sort of a disincentive for providing that longer care.” The government is reviewing the way it costs individual consultations for different issues, through a review of the Medicare Benefits Scheme. Health Minister Mark Butler said the increased bulk-billing rates were “good for patients’ hip pockets and good for their health”. “Across the country more and more GP practices are becoming fully bulk-billing clinics meaning all patients need is their Medicare card, not their credit card,” he said.

World.title: Katrina Taylor’s breast implants made her sick. This new device could make women feel whole again
World.content:
Exclusive NationalScience Katrina Taylor’s breast implants made her sick. This new device could make women feel whole again Kate Aubusson August 10, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

About 15 years ago, an email from a PhD student with a bold idea dropped into the inbox of Professor Anand Deva. “It said something like: I’ve got this idea about using an absorbable breast scaffold to encourage tissue regeneration,” Deva recalled. ‘I wanted to help’: Katrina Taylor, a participant in a clinical trial for 3D-printed breast scaffolds. Audrey Richardson The plastic and reconstructive surgeon had not yet become a beacon for women with breast implant complications. But they would soon come from across Australia and overseas with ruptures, infections and a constellation of symptoms linked to breast implant illness. The student, Mohit Chayya, was pitching a solution for a problem that would soon inundate Deva’s practice: women with silicone breast implant complications, ruptures, infections and a constellation of breast implant illness symptoms.



“My reply was: Yeah, yeah, best of luck. Call me in 10 years when you’re ready for patient trials,” said Deva, the Head of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery at Macquarie University. Related Article Investigation

Medical misogyny ‘These mistakes cost lives’: The medical bias that affects half of Australia A world-leading researcher in breast surgery complications and safety, Deva knew that there were myriad hurdles between idea and approved medical device. But on Monday, Deva will use 3D-printed scaffolds for the first time on women who have never had silicone implants in a pivotal trial to assess their safety and performance. “Now I’ve swooped in for the glory,” joked Deva of the trial sponsored by the scaffold’s medtech company, BellaSeno.



Forty-two Australian women have had their silicone implants replaced with the half-moons of white lattice, their bodies acting as bioreactors as the scaffold slowly dissolves, leaving behind their own regenerated fat tissue. Ultimately, the researchers and Chayya – BellaSeno’s co-founder and chief executive – say they hope the scaffolds will offer breast cancer patients an alternative after lumpectomies and mastectomies. “The end goal for us is to help patients like my grandma, who have no options,” Chayya said of his grandmother, Bansari, who lived with a deformity left by a lumpectomy to treat breast cancer in Gujarat, India. “I could see the struggle that she had mentally and psychologically,” he said. The scaffold’s crisscross pattern of bands and tiny filaments is made of a polymer called polycaprolactone, which has been used for decades in absorbable sutures used to stitch up wounds and surgical incisions.



“It’s 90 per cent porous,” Chayya said. The smallest size – 100 cubic centimetres – weighed 10 grams. Professor Anand Deva shows the 3D-printed breast scaffold in a medical library in Sydney. Audrey Richardson The procedure is similar to that of silicone implants, but with an extra step. The surgeon uses liposuction to harvest fat from the patient’s abdomen, buttocks or thighs and injects it into the scaffold, filling up to 50 per cent. “Fat is a cocktail of a lot of really good cells – growth factors, small blood vessels and stem cells, which grow and multiply along the scaffold, filling up the remaining space,” Chayya said. The body gradually absorbs the scaffold over two to three years, leaving just the tissue. “The regenerative process is incredible,” Deva said, “[unlocking] the body’s own capacity to heal and produce its own tissue with no footprint of the thing a year or two later.”



The lightness of the scaffold surprised trial participant Katrina Taylor as she palmed the device in Deva’s office. Five months after undergoing the procedure, Taylor said she forgets they’re in there. “If I touch [my chest], they feel firm because they haven’t absorbed yet … they look so natural,” she said. Taylor was 36 when she got her first set of breast implants after having children. A decade later, they had ruptured, causing severe chest pain.



She would have two breast implant revisions. Then she developed a procession of alarming symptoms: pleurisy (inflammation of the membrane lining the lungs and chest wall) that caused stabbing pains, frequent migraines, fatigue, extreme hair loss, body rashes, sore joints, muscle weakness and bowel problems. “I was 53 years old, and I felt like I was going crazy,” Taylor said. “No one could give me any answers, and I was at the stage where I thought: I don’t know if I can do this any more.” Taylor recognised her symptoms in a news article about breast implant illness. “I thought, I’ve got to have them out,” Taylor said. Within months of her explant surgery with Deva: “I was back to my normal self”. Taylor was eager to take part in the trial: “If there’s something else that could give women other options, I wanted to help,” she said.



Professor Anand Deva and Katrina Taylor, a participant in the clinical trial. Audrey Richardson Reconstructive surgeon Professor Owen Ung has performed 19 breast augmentations with the BellaSeno scaffold on women who had silicone implants as part of a phase 1 safety trial with a two-year follow-up. “These patients didn’t have an alternative because they were having all sorts of trouble with their implants,” said Ung, Director of the Comprehensive Breast Cancer Institute at Metro North Health. “When you remove an implant, you don’t always go back to what you would have looked like beforehand,” Ung said. “Older women can be left with quite a big defect from where the implant used to be,” and not all women have enough fat for a fat transfer augmentation. “I can see hundreds of thousands of women across the world having these.” Ung said.



The trial results – presented at an Australasian Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons conference in Boston in May have not yet been submitted for peer review – found participants retained 83 per cent of their breast volume since their surgeries, and there were no serious adverse events. Related Article Healthcare Experts sound warning over influencers fracturing their ribs for smaller waists Dr Tony Connell, a leading plastic and reconstructive surgeon in Perth, said the trial results were impressive, and he was hopeful that the scaffolds could be an invaluable option. “There will be patients not suited for this who need more volume than the scaffolds can provide ... but imagine if I could say to women: ‘we could take our implant out and safely put in a bio scaffold and your own fat’. It’s a very promising thing.” First it was critical to ensure the researchers discovered what the scaffolds looked like with imaging to detect one of the most common cancers in women.



“It stands to reason that some women with scaffolds will get breast cancer, and we need to be able to investigate them in the same way we would anybody else,” Ung said. A total of 106 women will take part in the pivotal trial, including three-monthly MRI scans. Deva’s surgery on Monday marks the next step in safety and performance testing, expanding the trial to 53 women who have never had implants. The 3D-printed scaffold uses fat cells to replace breast implants. Audrey Richardson “We’re not there yet,” said Deva, also the Director of the Integrated Specialist Healthcare Education & Research Foundation (ISHCERF).



“No device should be rushed to market without adequate independent scientific and clinical evaluation,” he said, recalling the significant harm caused to women with transvaginal mesh, which bypassed rigorous clinical trials. “This is not about replacing silicone implants, which serve the majority of women very well ... It’s about giving them another option.” Pending trial results and Therapeutic Goods Administration approval, Chayya hoped the scaffolds could be available for women after implant removal from 2028, followed by women who never had implants. Nick Daicos racked up 21 disposals, five clearances, one goal and a goal assist in a monster first half, and he continued to dominate in the third term as Collingwood broke the game open. AAP

World.title: Two arrested after fleeing vehicle collides with police car
World.content:
Two people have been arrested after a car crashed into two vehicles, including a police car, and swerved around road spikes near Palmerston North this evening.

Whanganui Area Commander Inspector Ash Gurney said police sighted a vehicle of interest in the Marton area about 4.30pm, and signalled for it to stop.

"The driver failed to do so, and officers did not pursue due to the manner of driving."

Inspector Gurney said the vehicle then fled towards Whanganui on State Highway 3.

"Officers set up road spikes. However, the vehicle avoided them and continued to flee. Due to the manner of driving and associated risks, officers did not pursue the vehicle."

Leaving Whanganui, the vehicle collided with a police car at low speed.

No injuries were reported, but the police car was damaged to the point that it was undriveable.

Police sighted the vehicle again about 6pm travelling south through Bulls and more attempts to spike the vehicle were unsuccessful.

About 6.25pm, police said the vehicle was involved in a crash near Levin, but continued driving. No injuries had been reported.

Just after 7pm, police received a call reporting the vehicle had hit a fence at Rangiotu, and two occupants were taken into custody.

World.title: St John confirms weekly all-time call record has been broken again
World.content:
A spike in winter illnesses is being blamed for Hato Hone St John recording its busiest single day on record.

The ambulance service has now activated its major incident response to cope with sustained high demand, which was expected to continue on Monday.

On Saturday, 2562 calls came into the ambulance service through 111 - the highest number received in a single day. A normal day would see around 1900 calls. There were 2079 calls to 111 for an ambulance by 5.45pm on Sunday.

As of 7.45pm on Sunday, the ambulance service had received 16,008 calls this week. That beat the previous record of 15,289 calls, set just a week earlier between 27 July and 2 August.

Before that, the busiest week on record had seen 14,984 calls. That record was set between 25 and 31 August in 2025.

Hato Hone St John director of ambulance operations Doug Gallagher said the "highly unusual" sudden spike in demand correlated with the recent cold snap, and there had been an influx in people requesting ambulances for winter illnesses such as influenza and respiratory issues.

"It has been a relatively mild winter, up until about a week, a week and a half ago.

"There does seem to be a correlation with the temperature, the weather. So from that perspective, there's a bit of hope that when the weather improves things can get back to normal."

While patients with broken bones, those who had fallen, and those not in life-threatening pain could expect to wait several hours for an ambulance, Gallagher said response times for the sickest patients remained within safe limits.

"During that time, though, all incidents are being managed and monitored. They are likely to receive callbacks from clinicians within our 111 centre and potentially, the problem can be managed over the phone with clinical advice or referral into other parts of health."

He said about 10 percent of the calls they received were dealt with over the phone, through a process called Hear and Advise.

On Saturday, 2562 calls came into the ambulance service through 111. St John / Supplied

Emergency services under pressure

Gallagher explained the ambulance service's concerns at a press conference on Sunday afternoon, where St John confirmed the major incident response following a difficult Saturday.

"At the peak, emergency call handlers were answering a call every 20 seconds," he said.

Multiple days in the past week "were busier than any recorded during the Covid-19 pandemic or on traditionally high-volume dates such as New Year's Eve", he said.

"Our emergency ambulance staff are continuing to respond effectively, but the workload is not showing the signs of easing that we would normally expect," he said on Sunday afternoon.

World.title: Wellington city councillor Tony Randle dies suddenly
World.content:
Local and national politicians are paying tribute to Wellington city councillor Tony Randle, who died suddenly at the weekend.

Councillor Randle, who represented the Takapū/Northern Ward, was first elected in 2022 and re-elected in 2025.

He served on a number of committees and was appointed to the Wellington Regional Transport Committee. Earlier this week he voted with city councillors agreed to submit a super-merger proposal to the government this weekend.

Wellington mayor Andrew Little said Randle's contribution to the council was marked by diligence, care and a commitment to understanding the detail.

"Tony was deeply committed to public service and wanted the best for Wellington and its communities. He was always cordial and constructive, but he also brought a healthy scepticism to every issue.

"He believed an important part of his role was to challenge, question, and test assumptions to ensure decisions were based on solid evidence.

"What really set him apart was his focus on substance over rhetoric. He wanted to understand the facts, examine the evidence, and make the best possible decision based on all available information.

"He was never willing to be rushed and valued thorough analysis and quality decision-making above all else. He applied his analytical skills to public transport in particular and was always willing to engage with the public on detailed and principles grounds."

He would be sorely missed around the council table, Little said.

"He was just one of those people that you knew when he was in a meeting, he was onto it, he was going to ask questions and he was all about ... doing the best that he could."

Little said discovering a $250 million error in council consultation documents on lowering the speed limit in 2023 exemplified his determination to dig into the details.

"He very much focused on the data and if he didn't think he had enough would ask for more, and what he found through that process and his hard work was that actually they had miscalculated some of the data and had come up with a conclusion that was out by $250 million."

There would be a by-election for councillor Randle's seat in due course, Little said.

Infrastructure Minister and Hutt South MP Chris Bishop described councillor Mr Randle as a lovely man who was passionate about Wellington.

Council chief executive Matt Prosser said Randle was a "strong and passionate advocate for his local community, engaging thoughtfully with residents and participating in public discussions on issues that mattered to Wellington".

World.title: Schools closed as Ohakune faces water shutdown
World.content:
Ohakune schools will be closed on Monday as the town grapples with a water shutdown caused by leaking pipes.

The Ruapehu District Council and water contractor Veolia are urging residents to conserve water, warning the town's reservoir is down to 12 percent.

A council spokesperson said the leak, caused by last month's earthquake, was discovered on Thursday and repaired the following day, but the need to remove air from the water line had delayed the fix.

The council had brought in port-a-loos and was providing tankers of drinking water, but stressed that they were for homes and essential services, and businesses may need to close.

"The reservoir has been drained, so it takes time for that reservoir to refill and then for the treatment to come through," Horizons Regional Council chair Nikki Riley said.

"But until then, the good people of Tongariro Water will be supplying water for the township."

Tap water was not expected to be restored until 5pm Monday. If restored before then, the water would need to be boiled before use, the council said.

It warned against using public toilets.

Drinking water was available at various locations around the town, it said.

Nearly 1400 people live in Ohakune, but the population can double or treble during the ski season.

Drinking water

Bottled water: Ruapehu District Council office, 38 Ayr St; Thames St opposite the Powderhorn; Goldfinch St/Shannon St corner; rear car park of the Ohakune iSite; Clyde St car park; Moore St outside Top 10 Holiday Park.

Water tanker: Council office. Please reuse empty 5-litre bottles and refill them there.

World.title: Companies must adapt to rising AI costs, tech commentator says
World.content:
The cheap or free use of AI tools is over.

"For the last three years, the most expensive experiment in technology history has run on someone else's money," Fusion5 chief executive Kristy Brown said.

A white paper released by technology services provider Fusion5 sets out the case for a managed approach to the running of AI agents in order to avoid runaway costs, while maintaining compliance with emerging regulatory requirements as well as institutional risks to businesses.

"Who's paying for AI now? Increasingly, it's you," Brown said, adding that many AI agents were adopting a pay-by-token system rather than an all-you-can-eat user licence, or a hybrid scheme which combined a bit of both.

These include Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, Microsoft's CoPilot and many other widely used coding and customer service agents.

"Prior to this phase of our AI revolution, initially it was just about trying to get people to trust and to use AI," Brown said.

She said the challenge now was to use AI more efficiently, with smart processes that improved search accuracy and resulted in fast results.

"Usage-based pricing means every prompt, every reasoning step and every autonomous agent now carries a real, metered cost - and someone must pay it," she said.

"Autonomous agents now commit spend, reconcile transactions and make decisions that bind the organisation. They're also expensive in a way traditional software never was."

She said AI agents reason in loops and can consume an order of magnitude beyond a simple query.

"An agent stuck in a reasoning loop… can generate substantial costs before anyone notices."

She said AI agents needed monitoring and controls or risked landing businesses with a large bill and a nasty governance surprise.

"The businesses that build the discipline to operate AI - not just deploy it - will be the ones still standing when the music, and the free money, stops."

She said the key to improved performance was to collect key business processes in an "ontology", which was industry jargon for a rich, structured description of the underlying business model, including relationships to such things as a company description, the names and titles of senior executives, financial results, and small details like the font and colour of the business brand.

"It's the stuff that sits in your very deep experts' heads.

"And if you take the time to get those things right, it's a fast track way for your AI workloads to be able to get to the end outcome without a lot of these reasoning steps that it has to do if you haven't told it explicitly where to reference that information."

Brown said companies with incomplete data or digitised institutional knowledge were paying to ask AI agents to look for information that wasn't available, beyond the knowledge held by experienced staff.

"Without a shared meaning layer, businesses pay twice: once for the extra compute, and again for the mistake."

She said the transformation was already underway.

Global giants Tesla, Uber, Meta and Amazon were already implementing employee restrictions on AI Agent usage as businesses shift to the traditional model of measuring costs against productivity gains.

"The four biggest US tech firms are on track to spend close to US$700 billion on AI infrastructure this year alone. OpenAI reportedly spends around US$60 billion a year on compute against roughly US$13 billion of revenue. That gap has been a gift to the rest of us," Brown said.

"That gift was being withdrawn."

Microsoft was leading the pack in driving revenue gains through licensing of its AI Agent Copilot, which was an integral piece of its suite of Office tools, according to its latest fourth quarter earnings report.

"This year, Azure revenue surpassed US$100 billion for the first time, and Microsoft 365 Copilot reached over 30 million paid seats, reflecting the confidence customers are placing in us to power their AI transformation," Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said.

Global giants Tesla, Uber, Meta and Amazon are already implementing employee restrictions on AI Agent usage. Moor Studio

The case for an agent operations centre (AOC)

Brown said there was a case for a dedicated function that watched every agent in real time, tracked cost per agent with thresholds and alerts, monitored each agent's guard rails, and escalated to a human the moment an agent stepped out of line.

"This is exactly why Fusion5 is investing in building an Agent Operations Centre," Brown said, adding the service would be officially launched in the fourth quarter of the year, with 1400 existing customers in the New Zealand and Australian region.

She said an AOC was aimed at helping small to mid-sized businesses, who don't have the in-house expertise to manage themselves.

"For a business without Silicon Valley's balance sheet, that math matters even more."

She said the proliferation of AI assistants or agents had introduced a class of operational challenges that conventional IT management was never designed to address.

"Business functions that rely on autonomous agents for critical workflows cannot simply revert to manual processes when agents fail or are unavailable," the white paper says.

World.title: Deadline for local council amalgamation plans arrives
World.content:
The future of New Zealand's councils is now in the government's hands, with time running out to submit an amalgamation proposal.

Sunday was the deadline to pitch a Head Start plan for creating larger unitary councils.

Those who have not done so will now have one forced on them under the Back Stop process.

Officials will now assess the proposals - including whether it is realistic and delivers better value to ratepayers.

Approved plans will be signed off in 2027, with the Back Stop process finalised in the same year.

The changes are expected to take effect from the 2028 local elections.

City v rural

Earlier this week, Hamilton District Council voted 12 to three to not participate - meaning the district would end up in a backstop process controlled by central government to ensure reforms still went ahead. Down south, Christchurch City Council unanimously agreed to submit on the Head Start process. Wellington and Wairarapa mayors have agreed to put two amalgamation proposals to ministers.

In the Manawatū-Whanganui, five councils have agreed to work together on a work programme, rather than submit a plan for amalgamation.

Palmerston North and Horowhenua have proposed a new sub-regional council, but Whanganui mayor Andrew Tripe says it - along with Rangitīkei, Tararua, Manawatū, and Ruapheu - have chosen an alternative option.

Tripe said the council was not going to let the government decide what it was going to do.

He said it was not against local government reform, but needed more time to consult with the community, as well as consider what financial constraints the council would face.

Nearly 90 percent of those surveyed by Manawatū District Council were opposed to amalgamating.

Mayor Michael Ford said 86 percent of the 750 people who responded to the survey were against amalgamating with any other councils in the Manawatū-Whanganui region.

He said more than half refused to answer who they would prefer to join with if forced, while 30 percent voted for Rangitīkei, and 10 percent for Palmerston North.

Ford said Manawatū's rural community were very opposed to amalgamating with Palmerston North, as they did not want city people telling them how to run their farms.

On announcing the three-month Head Start process in May, Local Government Minister Simon Watts and Resource Management Act Reform Minister Chris Bishop had a stark message for councils.

"Today we are giving council's a clear choice. Lead your own reform or we will do it for you," Bishop said.

In a post on social media this morning, former prime minister Helen Clark said it had been a "haphazard approach" to local government amalgamation, driven by current government.

World.title: 'Great concerns' for missing Whanganui woman, police say
World.content:
Police are seeking help from the public to find a 59-year-old woman reported missing from Whanganui.

The woman, Sharon, was last seen on Monday, 27 July around 11am, near Kent Road in Saint Johns Hill.

"Police and Sharon's family have great concerns for her welfare and would like to find her as soon as possible," authorities wrote in a post on social media on Sunday.

"We believe she is still in the Whanganui area, however she has links to Auckland, and could also be in the wider Auckland area."

World.title: Munster free to play after dangerous contact charge downgraded
World.content:
Melbourne Storm five-eighth Cameron Munster has avoided suspension after the NRL Match Review Committee downgraded his dangerous contact charge from Saturday's win over Manly.

Munster was initially facing a week on the sidelines, and two if he unsuccessfully challenged the charge, for a low tackle at the knees of Sea Eagles prop Taniela Paseka.

The Storm star was the third man in to the tackle, targeted the legs of Paseka, and left the Manly big man in pain.

Paseka was helped from the field, and Munster was charged with a grade two dangerous contact.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

But the MRC has now downgraded that to a grade one, after receiving a medical report that shows Paseka's injury may not be as bad as first feared.

A statement from the NRL says new information warranted the charge being downgraded, which means Munster can cop a $750 fine for pleading guilty.

"When initially ascribing a grading to Melbourne Storm's Cameron Munster for the charge of dangerous contact, the MRC considered the contents of a medical report provided by the injured player’s club, which offered preliminary details as to the nature and extent of the injury," the NRL statement said.

"Subsequently, the match review committee has received a further report which materially alters the nature and extent of the injury suffered by the player.

"Pursuant to Rule 61 of the NRL Judiciary Code, where further expert or medical information warrants a different grading, the match review committee may authorise the match review manager to amend the grading and issue an amended notice of charge.

"Following due consideration of this report, the match review committee has reviewed the charge against Cameron Munster and, in accordance with the judiciary code, has forwarded the player an amended notice of charge for the offence of dangerous contact (grade 1)."

Munster made his return to action following a knee injury in the Storm's win over the Sea Eagles in Perth, keeping alive their very slim finals hopes.

The Storm have the bye next week, then must win their remaining three matches starting with a clash against Penrith at AAMI Park.

Even if the Storm win their remaining three matches, they will need other results to go their way.

World.title: Rising Aussie UFC star calls for tougher fighters after first-round win
World.content:
The moment was not too big for Quillan Salkilld.

Making his main event debut, the Australian's run of first-round finishes continued on Saturday night local time in Las Vegas as he defeated veteran Mateusz Gamrot with a rear-naked choke at 4:25 of the first round of their non-title lightweight bout at UFC Fight Night at the UFC APEX.

Salkilld (13-1) survived a Gamrot (26-5) leg-lock during an extensive grappling exchange in the scheduled five-round fight before working to the back and locking in the finish, earning the biggest victory of his career while extending his winning streak to 13 fights.

Salkilld, who has now won his past four fights and five of his last six in the first round, called for a step up in competition after the victory.

"I think I deserve someone who's in the top five or close to it," Salkilld said.

Following the victory, the number 12-ranked Salkilld positioned himself for a match-up near the top of the lightweight division, while the number eight-ranked Gamrot absorbed a setback against one of the division's fastest-rising contenders.

Saturday's event marked the UFC's return to Las Vegas after two events abroad, in Abu Dhabi on July 25 and then Belgrade last Saturday.

In the co-main event, Diego Ferreira (20-7 MMA) landed more than 135 significant strikes across 15 minutes to earn a unanimous decision against Billy Quarantillo (18-8 MMA) in their lightweight bout.

All three judges scored the fight 30-27 for Ferreira, who kept Quarantillo on the defensive in Quarantillo's first Octagon appearance in more than 600 days after suffering a knee injury and his first lightweight fight since 2017.

Darren Elkins's UFC retirement fight ended unceremoniously as Yadier del Valle (11-1 MMA) needed one left hook to secure a TKO stoppage 35 seconds into the opening round of their featherweight bout.

Del Valle quickly closed the show against Elkins (29-13 MMA), spoiling the longtime veteran's final Octagon appearance while rebounding from the first loss of his career in February.

"I'm thankful for it all … don't ever give up on yourself," Elkins said following the loss.

Strawweight Alexia Thainara (15-1) utilised a relentless pace and a variety of take-downs alongside unorthodox striking to earn a unanimous decision against former strawweight contender Amanda Lemos (15-7-1), taking the cards 29-28, 29-28 and 30-27 in their all-Brazilian match-up.

Unbeaten welterweight Ty Miller (8-0 MMA) opened the main card by stopping Billy Ray Goff (9-5 MMA) via TKO 15 seconds into the third round.

Miller unleashed punches against the fence to force the stoppage, extending his perfect professional record while handing Goff his third straight defeat.

Reuters

World.title: Raiders bemoan 'f***ing brain explosion' as their season ends
World.content:
The Dragons beat the Sharks 24-16 in a thrilling derby victory at Kogarah, as the Knights ended the Raiders season with a 30-24 victory in Canberra.

Trailing 26-24 in the final 10 minutes of the contest, the Raiders were awarded a penalty after Dane Gagai and Corey Horsburgh tangled at a play the ball.

Instead of having a kick at goal to level the scores though, Horsburgh slapped Gagai over the head, resulting in the penalty being overturned.

Ricky Stuart was livid, calling the incident "a f***ing brain explosion".

"We should have gone 26-all and there was a brain explosion," Stuart said.

"It was a f***ing brain explosion, and we lost the opportunity."

Stuart was under no illusions that his forward was in the wrong, either.

"Of course it was [a sin bin]," he said.

"There was one last week. Everyone knows that, you're not allowed to do that. It's in the rules. It's been in the rules for the last many, many years."

The Raiders fans may have felt hard done by after Gagai was not sin binned earlier in the half following a tip tackle on Horsburgh, for which he was only placed on report by referee Ashley Klein.

In the late match, St George Illawarra dealt Cronulla Sutherland's top-two finals hopes a hammer blow with a spirited 24-16 victory.

The Dragons and Sharks engaged in a brutal first half. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

Recording only their third win of the season and just their second derby success in their last 13 against the Sharks, the Dragons are still in the hunt to avoid the wooden spoon.

Addin Fonua-Blake could face a spell on the sidelines for the Sharks, after being sin binned and placed on report for nasty shoulder charge on Dragons forward Hamish Stewart.

Jesse Ramien left the field with a suspected pectoral injury and Ronaldo Mulitalo also played out the second half under an injury cloud on a bad afternoon for the premiership aspirants.

Meanwhile, Storm halfback Cameron Munster was given a one-match ban for dangerous contact against Sea Eagles forward Taniela Paseka, only to have that overturned a couple of hours later.

Munster was charged after making contact with the side of the knee of the Sea Eagles prop as the third man into a tackle during the first half of the game, which the Storm came from behind to win.

The NRL judiciary later amended the charges after a medical report from Manly showed Paseka's injury was not as severe as it was initially thought.

Instead of a week off, Munster can now accept a $750 fine for a grade one dangerous contact charge.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Australia's 999th Wallaby on his injury-riddled road to Test debut
World.content:
Isaac Henry will run the prospect of fresh ink past his wife but is otherwise assured he can make a permanent Wallabies mark after a hard-earned debut in Osaka.

Named on the bench, the Queensland Reds centre was made to wait more than 70 minutes before being thrust into the action and then defending furiously in a 35-32 Saturday night defeat of Japan.

The 27-year-old became Wallaby number 999 in the process, the honour coming despite Henry enduring four major surgeries in as many years.

Wallabies survive scare as Kiss era begins with win New Wallabies coach Les Kiss says his side will need to learn how to control their ambitions after Australia hangs on to win a frantic Test match against Japan in the Osaka heat.

"It's a great number, might have to talk to my wife about getting it tattooed," said Henry, who has his surname inked on his forearm.

A broken foot, hamstring tear and two separate knee ligament and tendon ruptures have been his biggest setbacks.

Incredibly, his six games for the Reds this season are more than he has managed in any campaign since his 2021 Super Rugby debut.

"It's been a journey … and there was a brief period where I was like 'maybe I won't get on, maybe next week'," he said of his nervous sideline wait.

Henry's patella tendon rupture in 2024 was a gruesome injury that left him sucking on the green whistle as he left the ground.

"I said [to myself], 'Right, I'm going to be back better than I was before'," he said of that setback.

"It's nice to be here … you look back at those days and think 'how good'.

"Deep down I'm stubborn; I wasn't going to quit, I wanted it too much, ever since I was a kid. And I set my mind to it."

Henry can kick off the tee and out of the hand and boasts a strong carry, good hands and a sharp football brain, according to coach Les Kiss.

Loading Instagram content

Hunter Paisami impressed at No.12, while outside centre Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii set up one try but didn't have the impact he threatened to.

The debutant is confident he can thrive if given more opportunities in Townsville's Japan rematch on Saturday.

"There were points along the way that I didn't think I'd get it done, but now I've got a taste and I'm hungry for it," Henry said.

"I loved it and now I've sort of experienced that I just want more. Loved the next level, loved testing myself."

AAP

World.title: Blues plant one foot in the AFL finals as Saints lose star to hamstring
World.content:
Alright, we've got two games remaining in the season.

Let's work our way from the bottom up of the ladder to see where things stand.

Season over: The Bombers, Tigers, Eagles, Power and Suns will all be looking to the trade period and the draft now. The Suns were the most recent domino to fall despite their stirring win over the Giants today.

North Melbourne: The Kangaroos are highly unlikely to play finals, two games behind Carlton in the wildcard position in 10th, with a poor percentage and games against Geelong and Sydney to come. Put a line through them, they're done.

GWS Giants: The close loss to the Suns today have absolutely devastated GWS hopes of making a wildcard spot. They're two games behind the Blues, and while they should account for the Eagles, they then face an away trip to Adelaide to face the Crows. They'd need to win both and hope the Blues drop both their games, and the Saints drop at least one.

St Kilda: Two games behind the Blues. That's bad. Winnable games against the Tigers and the Suns. That's good. Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera definitely out for both of those games. That's bad. On balance it looks unlikely the Saints will wedge their way into a wildcard spot, but ...

Carlton: The Blues face tough matches against the Bulldogs and the Dockers to finish the season. They drop both of those, and the Saints win both of theirs, and St Kilda would leapfrog Carlton on percentage.

The rest: All other teams are locked into finals, but it's tight around which teams play in the wildcards, and which teams can force their way into the top four. The Dockers will have a home qualifying final, and it's unlikely the Swans will be moved out of second with a strong percentage and a soft finish against the Kangaroos and the Bombers.

Brisbane and Melbourne look like the likeliest teams to round out the top four with Adelaide facing a tough trip to Perth against Fremantle next week, but don't rule out the Cats, who face the Kangaroos and Tigers in their final two weeks.

It's going to be a belter of a finish and after all this talk of the wildcard spots being the exciting part of the ladder, the old top-eight would be an incredible watch right now if it still existed.

World.title: Infantino denies 'defamatory' affair claims made in British newspaper
World.content:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who has endured a week of scathing criticism revolving around the now shelved private investment plan for the World Cup, has been accused by a British newspaper of paying off an alleged lover while at UEFA.

According to The Daily Telegraph, the Italian-Swiss lawyer, who served as secretary general of European football's governing body from 2009 to 2016, also previously used his influence to secure a promotion for the same UEFA employee with whom he was in an intimate relationship.

Infantino has categorically denied the allegations, according to the article which was published late on Friday.

When contacted by AFP on Saturday, a FIFA spokesperson had not responded.

According to The Telegraph, which did not cite its sources, this employee received a "a six-figure sum" upon her departure – at an unspecified time – in addition to the payment of tuition fees for a business school amounting to around 45,000 British pounds ($85,900).

Gianni Infantino (right) in 2007 when he was UEFA's deputy general secretary. (Getty Images: Etsuo Hara)

When contacted by AFP, UEFA acknowledged that "a departure payment was made to the individual in question" at that time, "coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school".

However, it insisted "the payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time", before adding that "such regulations have been tightened since 2016".

Quoted by The Telegraph, a FIFA spokesperson stated that Infantino, who has been married since 2001, "strongly denies these allegations", which were "categorically untrue".

"Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," FIFA added.

"No employee at UEFA and FIFA has ever raised a complaint regarding Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."

Infantino, who is standing for re-election next March, has been embroiled in a crisis since the announcement late last month of his controversial — and ultimately abandoned — plan to open up the World Cup to private investors.

He faces opposition in particular from UEFA, which on Thursday stood by its threat to boycott the World Cups, deeming the mere withdrawal of the controversial plan to be insufficient.

Infantino maintains substantial support

Following a crisis meeting in Morocco on Wednesday, FIFA apologised to its 211 member associations for mistakes in the handling of the proposal and said its leadership had reaffirmed its full support for Infantino.

The fallout has cast a shadow over Infantino's bid for a fourth term at the FIFA Congress in Morocco next year. No clear candidate to challenge him has yet emerged.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino (left) has faced criticism from President of the Football Association of Norway Lise Klaveness (right). (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

UEFA has said it no longer has confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation President Lise Klaveness called for him to resign on Friday, saying he no longer had the institutional trust required to govern FIFA.

But Infantino continues to enjoy substantial support among FIFA's 211 members. The Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously backed his leadership on Thursday, while South America's CONMEBOL rejected any attempt to oust him that did not involve a vote of all FIFA members.

Mexico's football federation (FMF) also backed Infantino, despite its regional confederation CONCACAF having called for a "comprehensive reckoning" with his presidency.

"The FMF will neither recognise nor approve any process convened outside of that institutional framework," the Mexican federation said.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Australian Beacroft smashes U20 world record to continue golden form
World.content:
Australia's Isaac Beacroft has maintained his stunning golden streak with a record-breaking victory in the 5km race walk at the world athletics under-20 championships in the US.

Beacroft's sizzling win in Eugene, Oregon, follows his Commonwealth Games gold medal just over a week ago in the 10km race walk in Glasgow.

Victory in Oregon means he now has the prestigious world U20 championships and Commonwealth Games gold-medal double.

​Beacroft also broke the world record in Oregon at the famous Hayward Field, his time of 18:40.37 smashing more than seven seconds off the previous mark.

"I'm over the moon, I couldn't be happier," the Australian said after his stunning victory on Saturday (local time).

"I knew coming in it was going to be so hard. It definitely was pretty hard, so I'm just so happy to get it done.

"It's a massive relief. I felt a fair bit of pressure going into this one, you are a Commonwealth champion, [people think] surely it's a walk in the park to do juniors.

"It's definitely not. I have raced each race to its merits, I don't know what is harder.

"I'm stoked to have won both, that's all I can say on that.''

Beacroft's world-record time meant he beat silver medallist Huajia Pu by more than three seconds, the Chinese athlete clocking 18:43.70.

Third place went to Italy's Nicolo' Vidal, more than 12 seconds behind in a time of 18:56.19.

Despite the impressive nature of his victory, Beacroft said it was difficult to come straight from Glasgow to Oregon.

"I had a day or two after my race to try and freshen up,'' he said.

"I didn't really freshen up there, I went out with the Commonwealth Games boys and girls.

"I didn't go too hard on the partying, but there was some definitely done, then it was pretty rough to travel here.

"There was a delay with the plane, but I think getting here and getting around the whole team has given me a real lift."

In another impressive result, the Australian team of Thewbelle Philp, Zara Hagan, Grace Crowe and Emilia Reed won their heat of the women's 4x100m sprint.

World.title: 'Always by my side': Argentina mourns death of Jorge Messi
World.content:
Jorge Messi, the father of soccer star Lionel Messi, has died at a hospital in the central Argentina city of Rosario. He was 68.

The Rosario-based Club Atlético Newell's Old Boys announced his death in a social media post on Saturday that said he had undergone treatment in recent months for an unspecified illness.

The post described him as "the pillar and the person who, with vision, rigour and affection, supported the career of the best player of all time, alongside his wife, Celia Cuccittini".

Lionel Messi embraces his father Jorge Messi after the World Cup final in Qatar in 2022. (Getty Images: Robert Michael)

In a statement, the South American Football Confederation (CONMEBOL) also offered its condolences "with respect and affection for Lionel".

Lionel Messi led Argentina to a runner-up finish in this year's World Cup. In the team's first match, against Algeria, he was visibly emotional after scoring the first of his three goals. He said later that he wept for "a reason unrelated to sports".

"I went through some difficult, complicated days," he said.

"I am grateful to the delegation, to all my teammates, because they were always by my side wishing me strength so that I would be OK."

Media reports at the time outraged the Messi family, which days later released a statement confirming that "Jorge is experiencing a health issue", without specifying the nature of his condition.

"A person's health and the peace of mind of their loved ones should not be the subject of speculation or irresponsible media interest," according to the statement, which also expressed "discomfort at the lack of sensitivity, respect and scruples with which some people have treated a strictly private and family matter".

A minute of silence is held in memory of Jorge Messi, Leo Messi's father, during the FVG Cup match between Udinese Calcio and Nottingham Forest in Italy. The FVG Cup is a three team tournament that also includes Barcelona. (Getty Images: Mattia Radoni/NurPhoto)

Jorge Messi was a chemical technician and worked as a steelworker. He played soccer as a midfielder and reached the youth ranks of Newell's Old Boys but had to abandon the sport to complete his mandatory military service in Argentina.

He played a fundamental role in his third son's career, serving as his agent and managing his business affairs.

He was the one who travelled with a young Messi to Barcelona in the early 2000s for the trial that would open the doors to La Masia, the club's youth academy.

Lionel Messi made his professional debut in 2005 and went on to win eight Ballon d'Or awards. He led Argentina to the 2022 World Cup title.

Lionel Messi (back) poses with his family, including dad Jorge (centre) in 2003. (Getty Images: Marcelo Boeri/El Grafico)

"My dad was always by my side," Lionel Messi said in a 2007 interview with Radio del Plata.

"Sometimes I would lock myself in my room to cry when we arrived in Barcelona, or my dad would do the same without me seeing him, or thinking I didn't see him. We pretended we were both OK, but we weren't.

"My dad even asked me what I wanted to do when we were feeling down, if I wanted to stay or go back, and I wanted to stay, and he stayed with me."

His father negotiated the contracts with Barça and later his transfers to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami, while also managing the use of his famous son's image rights and his numerous investments in real estate, hotels and restaurants.

In 2013, father and son were accused by a Spanish prosecutor of trying to conceal earnings from the player's image rights. Jorge Messi paid more than 5 million euros ($8.1 million) on August 14 to cover alleged back taxes and interest.

In Rosario, a sign at the VIP Rosario restaurant, one of the Messi family's gastronomic ventures, indicated that it was closed for the day.

The president of Argentina's soccer federation, Claudio Tapia, on Saturday issued a lengthy statement in which he recognised Jorge Messi "for having raised a person of values: humble, respectful, and deeply committed to others".

The organisation ordered a moment of silence to be observed at all matches across all categories of Argentine soccer and mandated that players, referees and coaching staff wear black armbands.

Tech.title: Dropbox is a PC builder’s best friend
Tech.content:
In 2018 I bet my reputation and self-worth on a huge crowdfunded game design project. It could have been a failure for many reasons, but the one I became most worried about was losing all of the work that was stored locally on my home-built PC — a scenario that would have left a lot of people very upset and placed me in deep trouble. I wasn’t irresponsible, I had local backups, but at some point I found myself in custody of so many important files that it scared me. And no matter how many redundancies I could build at home, they’d all still be in the same place — a risky bet. So I bought a subscription to Dropbox. Years later, it’s still one of the best software subscriptions that I happily renew each year.

It was great to have all that work backed up in the cloud — both for peace of mind and because it made working with collaborators breezier, letting them upload stuff directly to my drive, and letting me transfer files up to 50GB in size. In quick order I had built a trove of incredible artwork and complicated InDesign, Photoshop, and Illustrator files. The original goal for my Dropbox configuration was to make sure I wouldn’t lose any data in a worst-case scenario, so I set it up to mirror everything living on my work partition. Eventually, I ran smack into a worst-case scenario. Not once, but twice.

I’m still not sure why, but my latest home-built PC chewed through two separate 2TB Samsung 970 Evo SSDs. It’s difficult to tell what went wrong with them, but in each case I woke up one morning to find when I tried to boot up that no drive could be detected. I can still feel my stomach trying to sink into the floor when I press that power button these days, never knowing if my drive had died in its sleep.

Fortunately, both times, after some process-of-elimination testing I learned that just the drive had gone bad and everything else in my system was A-OK. Maybe I should have ditched Samsung after the second disaster, but I’m now on an 2TB 990 Evo Plus. Knock on wood, this thing better not fail. That drive now costs almost twice what I originally paid for it thanks to our new outrageously priced world of parts.

My Dropbox bill is about $204 a year for a family plan ($17 a month), which includes up to six members. If you’re just in it for yourself you can get it for $9.99 a month billed yearly (about $120 a year), which comes with 2TB of storage. You can upgrade to 3TB for around $143 a year. That might be a tough sell for people who already have dozens of subscriptions, but I find it to be a decent price for excellent digital insurance.

There are other powerful options out there, especially for professionals working with heavy files or complicated workflows. Backblaze, for example, has a personal backup plan with unlimited data for $99 a year and no restrictions on file size. And, of course, if you live on the Mac, Apple iCloud Plus isn’t a bad option — especially if you’re already paying for an Apple One subscription. Even Adobe offers file backups through Creative Cloud if that’s your jam, but I would not recommend using that clunky software suite for anything other than doing the work you need to do.

I can’t recall a single time the service failed

I prefer Dropbox because the software works consistently well across multiple operating systems and is usually neither seen nor heard. The Windows client is snappy and I’ve found with a fast internet connection that its real-time syncing is efficient and painless. Anytime a file is modified in the partition I have mirrored in the cloud, Dropbox quietly begins uploading it and making changes to my mirrored files in the cloud. After using it for about eight years now I can’t recall a single time the service failed or faltered. It’s so fast and reliable I often forget it’s even there.

Now, for the important caveat: This might not work for you if you have poor internet speeds. It really depends on how much data you’re regularly moving around on your computer and how quickly you make changes to it. This could particularly be a problem for asymmetrical data plans that commonly boast lightning-fast download speeds while offering pathetic upload speeds. I’ve done fine averaging only about 20Mbps upload, but if you’re on something even lower you should try a free trial for a backup plan before committing. You can also find plenty of download time calculators online; at my gigabit download speed it usually takes around two hours to download the 1TB of files I have synced in the cloud.

And one more caveat: Putting everything (or even just many things) on your computer in the cloud isn’t for everyone, and I completely understand why many folks wouldn’t or shouldn’t do that for sensitive files. I once built local RAID drives and even airgapped storage systems to avoid having everything online. These things are still possible but getting more expensive by the day as storage prices spike. You’re the best judge of how and where your data should be protected.

That sinking feeling of potentially losing my whole PC? It was immediately followed each time by the assurance that I’d only lost a computer’s body and not its soul. When I got my PC back up and running with new storage, it ended up taking less time to resync all my files than it did to troubleshoot and install new hardware. I can almost hear Billy Crudup doing a Mastercard commercial in my head: New solid state drive, three hundred eighty-nine dollars. Yearly Dropbox subscription, two hundred and three dollars. Never worrying about losing your data? Priceless.

Tech.title: AI detectors are creating a new era of distrust
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more news about how AI is changing our daily lives, follow Emma Roth. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Long before ChatGPT became a thing, educators and editors frequently used anti-plagiarism tools to see if writers were being honest about their work. These tools work by comparing a written work against a database filled with content from across the web, scholarly articles, and more to check for matching sentences and phrases. Some, like Turnitin, offer a percentage that claims to illustrate how much of the student’s writing overlaps with other works. Between potential false positives and uncertainty about whether work was duplicated intentionally, some educators have backed away from using that particular tool.

But now, the hunt for copied content is evolving into a war on AI-generated work. As quickly as students have picked up ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot, teachers have adopted so-called AI detectors just as fast. A survey from the Center for Democracy and Technology found that 43 percent of sixth to 12th grade teachers in the US regularly used AI detectors between 2024 and 2025. Some universities already using Turnitin in their learning management systems found that the service automatically enabled AI detection when the tool launched in 2023.

Instead of comparing pieces of written content, AI detectors like GPTZero, Pangram, and the one created by Turnitin rely on their own AI models to guess whether something might not be human-written — a process that’s arguably even murkier than matching text on the web. As noted by GPTZero, AI detectors use an algorithm to analyze a text’s wording, rhythm, and structure, as well as to pick up on patterns in length and tone that may be more common in AI-written text. This relatively subjective evaluation isn’t as solid as something you could back up by matching text online, and can get tripped up by writers who speak English as a second language. Despite this, Turnitin has said that its AI detector falsely flags less than 1 percent of human-written content as AI, while Pangram claims its false positive rate is just 1 in 10,000. GPTZero claims it has a similarly low rate of mistaking human content for AI.

How it’s going

People online are already accusing each other of “sounding like AI,” but the ready availability of AI detection tools is only adding fuel to the LLM witch hunt. In some high-profile cases, AI writing accusations have directly impacted people’s livelihoods and reputations. Last month, the publisher Minotaur dropped a $2 million book deal over concerns that its author, Jerry Falade, used AI — something he vehemently denies.

There’s Thierry Rignol, a French national who sued Yale last year after a professor accused him of writing portions of his final exam with AI, resulting in a failing grade and a one-year suspension. The professor used GPTZero to scan Rignol’s writing for signs of AI, but the lawsuit argues that “AI surveillance and detection tools are known to unfairly target non-native English speakers” like Rignol. In February, a student at Adelphi University won a lawsuit against the school after his professor similarly claimed he used AI to write an essay. Though the lawsuit doesn’t say which AI tool the professor used to examine the student’s essay, Adelphi University has a licensing agreement with Turnitin.

As pointed out by the University of California, Los Angeles, AI detection tools are trained to pick up on patterns that could indicate AI use, such as repetitive terms and phrases, text that sounds too formal or informal, and nonsensical phrasing. Some, like QuillBot, also measure the “unpredictability” of text, as “AI tends to make the most ‘obvious’ or most common language choices as compared with human-produced writing,” according to UCLA. They may also look for sentence structure that remains the same throughout as another sign of AI. But these measurements aren’t indicative of AI on their own, as some people may just have a writing style with these qualities.

Even though Turnitin touts low false positive rates, it maintains that its tool “may not always be accurate” and shouldn’t be used to take actions against a student. Grammarly warns that users “should never rely on the results of an AI detector alone,” while GPTZero says “no AI detector can ever truly be 100% perfect.” OpenAI even shut down its own AI writing detector in 2023 due to low accuracy.

But AI writing accusations are still being flung across the web. Last week, in a video broadcast to the more than 3.5 million followers across his social channels, Ozzy Osbourne’s son, Jack, accused journalist and Verge contributor Kat Tenbarge of using AI to write an article for Rolling Stone, while flaunting the results from an AI detector, Getsolved, as “proof” of his claim. Tenbarge has refuted the claim in a video and a post on her website, but Osbourne hasn’t retracted his accusation or deleted the video, leaving Tenbarge to deal with the trolls.

There are numerous examples of false accusations, from writers to students, with many accusers failing to acknowledge the disclaimers that come along with some of these AI detection tools.

What happens next

The uncertainty surrounding AI detectors is enough for some educational institutions to stop using them altogether. Yale University, Johns Hopkins University, Vanderbilt University, Georgetown University, and others have disabled or restricted the use of AI detection tools. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology also warns that “AI detectors don’t work.”

Instead of relying on tools to weed out AI, many schools are encouraging educators to rethink their lessons. The University of Chicago, for example, suggests telling students to slow down their reading, breaking up longer writing assignments, and requiring students to reflect on their work. Stanford University says professors can consider holding assessments in classrooms, while MIT advises professors to leave room for students to disclose whether they used AI for help on an assignment, without penalty.

With AI becoming more prevalent in and outside the classroom, efforts to suss out what’s written by a human or a machine are ramping up as well. Some online platforms are only exacerbating suspicions surrounding AI use. Substack has built Pangram into its app, allowing users to scan blogs for suspected AI-generated content, while LinkedIn added a “seems like AI slop” button on posts. The result is a new era of distrust, where readers constantly question whether what they’re reading is AI and real human writers try their best not to sound like it.
